items.title: Potential contribution of enveloped virions to long-distance movement of plant rhabdoviruses.
items.abstract: Current models of plant virus movement are based largely on extensive studies of nonenveloped viruses, particularly those possessing positive-sense RNA genomes. In contrast, how enveloped, negative-sense RNA plant viruses access and transit through vascular tissues remains largely unexplored. Here, we aim to address this question using two rhabdovirus-host pathosystems: rice stripe mosaic virus (RSMV) infection of rice and tomato yellow mottle-associated virus (TYMaV) infection of Nicotiana benthamiana. Immunofluorescence staining of RSMV-infected rice tissues revealed that viral antigens were predominantly localized to vascular tissues, including both xylem and phloem. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that mature enveloped virions accumulated abundantly within xylem parenchyma cells. RSMV particles were also observed in two vascular conduits: xylem vessel lumens and sieve elements. Moreover, major viral structural proteins and morphologically intact virions were detected in xylem sap. Similarly, enveloped TYMaV virions were detected in both xylem vessel elements and phloem sieve elements of infected N. benthamiana plants. Furthermore, reverse genetics analyses demonstrated that a TYMaV matrix gene deletion mutant deficient in virion morphogenesis retained wild-type levels of cell-to-cell movement but was completely defective in long-distance movement. Together, these results indicate that intact rhabdovirus virions constitute an important mobile entity for vascular long-distance trafficking, with both phloem and xylem potentially contributing to systemic movement.
items.authors: Yang G, Deng Y, Liu Q, Lin W, Wang J, Xie L, Li Z.

items.title: Alleviating chromium (Cr) toxicity in maize (Zea mays L.) using oak wood biochar and carbon nanoparticles: impacts on growth, physiology, and stress responses.
items.abstract: The rising demand for food production necessitates innovative and sustainable agricultural practices, particularly in soils contaminated with heavy metals such as chromium (Cr). Oak wood biochar (OW-BC) and carbon nanoparticles (CNPs) have emerged as promising amendments for enhancing soil quality and plant health while mitigating Cr stress. This study explored the effect of OW-BC and CNPs on maize (Zea mays L.) growth, nutrient concentration, and soil enzymes under Cr stress (50 mg kg-1 Cr as total Cr) in a pot experiment. Results showed that OW-BC and CNP treatments increased shoot fresh weight by 30.2% and 28.0% without Cr stress, and by 34.1% and 28.4% under Cr stress, respectively, relative to the Cr treatment. Under Cr stress, OW-BC and CNPs improved shoot P concentration by 23.6% and 71.1%, respectively, relative to the Cr treatment, though shoot K concentration was not restored to control levels. Under Cr stress, both OW-BC and CNPs exhibited statistically non-significant, but numerically lower shoot Cr concentrations (by 8.1% and 10.0% compared with the Cr-alone treatment, respectively), as well as similar numerical increases in biomass (34.1% vs. 28.4%). The results in this study indicate that OW-BC and CNPs act as good soil conditioners and plant protectants to enhance plant tolerance to Cr toxicity and support sustainable crop production.
items.authors: Zulfqar A, Xin X, Saqib ZA, Bashir MH, Niazi NK, He Z.

items.title: Identification of auxin response factor ARF27 as a regulator of maize root morphogenesis.
items.abstract: Auxin is a central phytohormone that mediates root development. This study investigated the genetic basis of auxin-mediated primary root growth in Zea mays (maize) seedlings, which is not well-understood in this key cereal crop. To address this knowledge gap, 618 accessions from the Wisconsin Diversity panel were leveraged for a genome wide association study (GWAS) followed by reverse genetics and in silico gene regulatory network reconstruction (GRN). The GWAS identified several candidate genes associated with variation in root growth responses, including RAMOSA2 and multiple members of the AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR (ARF) gene family. Maize AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR27 (ZmARF27), an ortholog of Arabidopsis ARF7 and ARF19, was prioritized for functional characterization. A reduction in ZmARF27 levels led to short primary roots, insensitivity to exogenous auxin, and altered transcriptional responses. Reconstruction of an ZmARF27 GRN included known maize classical root development genes, such as ROOTLESS CONCERNING CROWN ROOTS, numerous auxin pathway genes, and genes associated with cell wall biogenesis. Altogether, this study identifies ZmARF27 as a novel genetic driver of auxin-mediated root growth and gene expression in maize.
items.authors: Dash L, Draves MA, Khangura RS, McReynolds MR, Muench RL, Cowling CL, Song G, Dilkes BP, Walley JW, Kelley DR.

items.title: ChZF7, a C3H zinc finger protein derived from alkaliphilic microalgae, improves alkaline stress tolerance in poplar via modulating flavonoid and hormone metabolism.
items.abstract: Soil alkalinity severely restricts plant growth, especially woody plants such as poplar. In this study, we identified ChZF7, a C3H-type zinc finger protein from alkaliphilic microalgae Chlorella sp. BLD, and explored its function in improving alkaline stress tolerance in Shanxin poplar (Populus davidiana × P. bolleana). Under alkaline stress, ChZF7 overexpression lines displayed superior growth status, reduced electrolyte leakage and less reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation relative to WT plants. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed that ChZF7 induces extensive metabolic reprogramming in poplar. Differentially expressed genes and accumulated metabolites were primarily enriched in the flavonoid biosynthesis pathway, along with the upregulation of genes and increased metabolites in the ABA biosynthetic pathway. Collectively, our results demonstrate that ChZF7 positively enhances alkaline tolerance in poplar by coordinating antioxidant metabolism, flavonoid metabolism and hormone metabolism. This work provides novel insights into alkaline stress adaptation mechanisms of woody plants, and highlights microalgae-derived zinc finger proteins as promising genetic resources for improving stress resistance in forest trees.
items.authors: Qu D, Zhou J, Wang H, Li W, Li S, Lv M, Zhang J, Wu F.

items.title: Tree- and stand-level factors associated with red turpentine beetle (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) damage in Chinese pine across infestation stages.
items.abstract: The red turpentine beetle (RTB), Dendroctonus valens LeConte (Coleoptera: Curculionidae), is an important invasive bark beetle affecting Chinese pine (Pinus tabuliformis Carrière) forests in northern China. However, whether the effects of tree- and stand-level factors on RTB damage vary across infestation phases remains unclear. Following a space-for-time substitution approach, we surveyed 468 sample trees from stands representing the incipient and epidemic phases of RTB infestation and measured 12 candidate tree- and stand-level factors. Univariate analyses and generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were used to identify factors associated with RTB damage across infestation phases. Damaged and healthy trees differed significantly in multiple factors during the incipient phase, whereas these differences were substantially reduced during the epidemic phase. GLMM analyses showed that sun-exposed trunk area proportion (STAP) was significantly positively associated with RTB damage, whereas understory vegetation cover and nearest infested-tree distance (NITD) were significantly negatively associated with RTB damage during the incipient phase, with STAP showing the strongest positive association. During the epidemic phase, only NITD remained significantly negatively associated with RTB damage. Overall, more measured tree- and stand-level factors were associated with RTB damage in the incipient-phase study area than in the epidemic-phase study area. These findings indicate that associations between local tree- and stand-level conditions and RTB damage may differ with infestation intensity and provide insights for RTB monitoring and management.
items.authors: Han S, Ze S, Chen L, Wang J, Gao L, Ma Y, Luo Y, Yang S, Zhan Z.

items.title: The cell polarity landscape in Arabidopsis male and female gametophytes
items.abstract: Plant cell polarity underlies the capacity to directionally transport auxin and other small molecules, but also precedes asymmetric cell division in the stomatal lineage. Except for specific contexts, mechanisms underlying cell polarization are poorly understood. Most insights on plant cell polarity have come from studies on flowering plant sporophytes, while no polar protein localization has yet been reported in flowering plant gametophytes, despite clear anisotropic growth and asymmetric cell divisions in this generation. Inspired by the identification of deeply conserved SOSEKI proteins and their associated partners that mark polar domains in bryophyte gametophytes and Arabidopsis sporophytes, we here investigate cell polarity in Arabidopsis gametophytes. We discover a rich landscape of polar domains throughout male and female gametophyte development, marked by one or more polar proteins. We find that successive steps in male gametophyte polarization can be mechanistically uncoupled, and the first polarization step precedes asymmetric cell division. Using ectopic expression, we find that there is a near-universal capacity for polar protein localization in gametophytes through a single polarity system. Our work offers the first insight into gametophyte cell polarity in Arabidopsis, identifies novel polar domains, and presents a starting point for future dissection of mechanisms underlying plant cell polarity.
items.authors: Koh Wee Han, S., van Schie, M., Albrecht, C., Ramalho, J., Voss, B., Weijers, D.

items.title: Phloem conductance from leaf to fruits in avocado during development
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Reproductive function in seed plants depends on efficiently allocating nutrients from sources to developing fruits. Hydraulic transport of carbohydrates largely depends on phloem architecture, but how phloem structure in fruit pedicels changes with development remains unexplored for most seed plants. Using the one-year phenology of avocado trees, we quantified water content, dry matter, and non-structural carbohydrates (NSCs) in mature leaves, flowers, young fruits, and fully developed fruits. Concomitantly, we measured phloem conduit geometry in different vein orders of leaves and in flower-fruit pedicels over time, including sieve tube numbers in cross sections. NSCs were below 5% in leaves and fruits but reached the highest concentrations in flowers, especially fructose (20%) and glucose (35%), and the pedicels of flowers showed the smallest conduits. While sieve tube elements in leaves scaled their geometry from the minor veins to the petioles, in fruit pedicels, their geometry changed only from flower to initial fruit set, increasing their number linearly up to fruit maturation. Our models show that phloem transport toward the flowers is impaired, but total conductance increases gradually due to phloemogenesis.
items.authors: Agullo-Samper, M., Ferrer-Blanco, C., Gonzalez, C. E., Gennis, S., Jensen, K. H., Losada, J. M.

items.title: Ecological niche and plantation composition differentially shape bacterial community composition and assembly across the root-soil continuum in Populus simonii plantations
items.abstract: Abstract Mixed plantations are widely established to restore degraded sandy landscapes, yet bacterial community patterns across roots and surrounding soils remain poorly understood. This study examined bacterial diversity, composition, inferred assembly patterns, environmental associations, and predicted functional potential in contrasting Populus simonii plantations. We analysed 60 composite samples from root (R), rhizosphere (RS), and non-rhizosphere soil (NRS) in four stands in the Kubuqi Desert, northern China. These comprised a P. simonii monoculture and mixtures with Salix psammophila , Caragana korshinskii , and Pinus sylvestris var. Mongolica , with five plots sampled per stand. Root communities exhibited lower richness and diversity and distinct taxonomic composition compared with the two soil compartments. PERMANOVA confirmed significant effects of both ecological niche ( F = 24.995, p = 0.001) than stand type ( F = 2.649, p = 0.005) on community composition, with niche showing the stronger association. Null-model classifications varied among sample groups. Homogeneous selection was the most frequently assigned category in most groups, whereas dispersal limitation accounted for a larger proportion of comparisons in the sampled P. simonii and C. korshinskii mixture. Co-occurrence patterns also varied across ecological niches and plantation types, with the rhizosphere showing the highest connectivity and mixed plantations generally exhibiting greater connectivity than the monoculture. Soil water content was strongly associated with bacterial community variation ( r² =0.815, p = 0.0005). Predicted KEGG and COG profiles varied among niche and plantation combinations, but no consistent functional response to mixed planting was observed. Together, these results reveal that bacterial taxonomic composition and community assembly responded to different ecological dimensions, ecological niche was more strongly associated with compositional differentiation, whereas assembly processes varied more clearly among the four sampled stands. This decoupling highlights the multidimensional organization of bacterial communities across the root-soil continuum in sandy plantations.
items.authors: Ren Y, Yang G, Su M, Guo X, Qiao S, Shang J.

items.title: Catabolism of jasmonoyl-isoleucine modulates maize development and defense responses.
items.abstract: Proper spatial and temporal accumulation of the phytohormone jasmonoyl-isoleucine (JA-Ile) requires precise control of both its biosynthesis and catabolism. Two pathways for JA-Ile catabolism are the conversion of JA-Ile to 12-hydroxy-JA-Ile (12OH-JA-Ile) by JA-Ile hydroxylases, and the reversible deconjugation of isoleucine from JA-Ile by amidohydrolases, followed by conversion of jasmonic acid to 11-hydroxy-jasmonic acid by jasmonate-induced oxygenases. JA-Ile hydroxylase activity is performed by enzymes of the cytochrome P450 94B (CYP94B) family. In this study, we generated single and double loss-of-function mutants of the two CYP94Bs of Zea mays (maize), the JA-Ile hydroxylase ZmCYP94B1 and its paralog ZmCYP94B12 and used these mutants in combination with in vitro and in vivo assays, to explore roles of these genes in JA-Ile catabolism, development, and defense in maize. In vitro assays showed both ZmCYP94B1 and ZmCYP94B12 have JA-Ile hydroxylase activity, and ZmCYP94B1 may also produce 12-carboxy-JA-Ile. Loss of function of both genes in maize leads accumulation of JA-Ile in unstressed leaves, and to enhanced resistance to the insect pest Spodoptera frugiperda and fungal pathogens Cochliobolus heterostrophus and Fusarium verticillioides. This study shows that the JA-Ile hydroxylase pathway plays an important role in JA-Ile catabolism and plant defense in maize. The zmcyp94b mutants also reveal that the genes have roles in regulating plant height and tassel architecture indicating that the ZmCYP94Bs contribute to balancing JA-Ile mediated growth-defense trade-offs.
items.authors: Liu H, Sorg A, Mendoza J, Gorman Z, Li QB, Cross M, Basset GJ, Hunter CT, McCarty DR, Suzuki M, Best NB, Block AK.

items.title: Drought responses in trees are context-dependent: the role of experimental design.
items.abstract: Drought is a major driver of vegetation change yet estimates of plant responses to drought are derived from experiments that vary widely in design. This raises an important question: to what extent do reported drought responses reflect biological processes rather than experimental context? We conducted a meta-analysis of drought experiments in Eucalyptus and Quercus, comprising 712 effect sizes from 160 studies and 106 species across photosynthesis, stomatal conductance, intrinsic water-use efficiency (iWUE), leaf water potential, soil water content and root-to-shoot ratio. We evaluated variation associated with growth environment, drought-imposition method, study duration and sample size, and tested whether experimental-design effects persisted after accounting for realised drought intensity, quantified from drought-induced changes in leaf water potential. Drought responses varied substantially among experimental contexts but realised drought intensity overlapped broadly among pot and field experiments and between binary and progressive dry-down treatments, demonstrating that these experimental categories did not correspond to fixed levels of water stress. Accounting for realised drought intensity substantially improved model fit and reduced the estimated difference between pot and field experiments, although experimental-design terms remained jointly significant, indicating that realised drought intensity did not fully account for variation associated with experimental context. Trait-specific responses also differed. Greater realised drought intensity was associated with increasingly negative photosynthetic responses, whereas the corresponding relationship for stomatal conductance was weaker, and no clear relationship was detected for iWUE. Sensitivity analyses identified the photosynthetic response to realised drought intensity as the most consistently supported trait-specific relationship. Our findings show that tree drought responses are context-dependent and that categorical experimental designs should be interpreted alongside the water stress experienced by plants. Incorporating realised drought intensity together with methodological context should improve cross-study comparisons and the interpretation of experimental drought responses.
items.authors: Singini EJ, Twala TC.

items.title: A developmentally scheduled inhibitory polarity circuit centers the stomatal pore
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Symmetry in living systems often arises from coordinated asymmetries at smaller scales. The guard cells of stomata--bilaterally symmetric epidermal valves that mediate plant-atmosphere gas exchange- -show coordinated asymmetries in pore placement and wall modification. Stomatal form and function are deeply conserved, yet molecular mechanisms defining coordinated cellular asymmetry are unknown. Here we show that pore position arises from a combination of pole avoidance and gradient centering in the membranes and wall dividing sister guard cells. Boundaries are established by spatiotemporal restriction of the receptor-like kinase MUSTACHES (MUS), which directs the disordered polarity protein OCTOPUS-LIKE2 (OPL2) to pore-forming regions. OPL2 peaks correspond to a focus of microtubules, and, from this position, the pore emerges. Experimental rewiring of the MUS-OPL2 polarity module profoundly impacts stomatal morphogenesis, eliminating, shifting, or even redirecting the pore to the opposite wall. These findings reveal a stomata-specific integration and elaboration of core polarity and centering programs, and challenge previous models of stomatal morphogenesis.
items.authors: Lebecq, A., Wallner, E.-S., Bergmann, D. C.

items.title: Temporal transcriptomic profiling reveals the positive role of NtWRKY40 in drought responses in tobacco.
items.abstract: Drought stress causes losses in crop yield and quality. The molecular mechanisms underlying plant drought responses have been extensively characterized in model plants. However, the regulatory mechanisms underlying drought response in tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) remain elusive. To uncover drought-responsive transcriptional dynamics, transcriptome sequencing was conducted on tobacco sampled at a series of time points under drought stress. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) yielded 27 drought-responsive modules. The pink module displayed a significant correlation with the early drought stress response, within which NtWRKY40 was characterized as a putative hub gene. NtWRKY40 was predominantly expressed in tissues at late developmental stages, and its protein localized to the nucleus. Compared with the wild type (WT), NtWRKY40-overexpressing tobacco exhibited improved drought tolerance, as evidenced by higher survival rates and maximum quantum efficiency of PSII (Fv/Fm), as well as lower levels of malondialdehyde (MDA), H2O2 and O2•-. The activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), and catalase (CAT) were higher in NtWRKY40-overexpressing lines, indicating enhanced ROS-scavenging capacity. Collectively, our results demonstrate that NtWRKY40 plays a positive role in drought tolerance, providing a promising genetic target for molecular breeding of drought-tolerant tobacco.
items.authors: Zhang H, Liu Y, Xu L, Du J, Zheng Q, Jin L, Liu P, Zhou H, Zhai N, Xu G.

items.title: Transcriptome analysis provides insights into candidate genetic regulators of birch response to salt stress
items.abstract: Background Soil salinization is a worldwide matter of concern and can result in a series of agricultural and ecological problems. Previous transcriptome data have shown genetic regulatory mechanisms of salt stress response in a salt-tolerant species of Betula halophila and a salt-sensitive species of B. platyphylla , but comparative analysis of transcriptional changes in the the two species remains limited. Aims We compared gene expression in leaves of B. halophila and leaves and roots of B. platyphylla . Methods Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified after 24 h of salt stress, followed by Gene Ontology enrichment and gene regulatory network (GRN) construction. Selected DEGs were examined by quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR). Results Compared with 0 h, 956 DEGs were found in B. halophila leaves (BHLeaf), 2,955 in B. platyphylla leaves (BPLeaf), and 3,827 in B. platyphylla roots (BPRoot). BHLeaf DEG expression patterns were similar to those of BPRoot. DEGs from BHLeaf and BPRoot were enriched in cell wall organization or biogenesis, whereas hormone biosynthesis and signaling genes were altered mainly in B. platyphylla . RT-qPCR showed that selected DEGs were induced by 200 mM NaCl for 24 h in B. platyphylla . Conclusions Our work uncovered genetic mechanisms of salt stress response commonly and uniquely occurring in two birch species and provides resources for breeding salt-tolerant birch. Highlights Salt stress altered the expression of 956, 2,955 and 3,827 genes in the two birch species. BHLeaf expression patterns were similar to those of BPRoot. The expression changes of nine selected DEGs were examined by RT-qPCR in B. platyphylla .
items.authors: Li, Z., Huang, Q., Li, L., Yan, L., Zhou, B., Jie, C.

items.title: Compost-associated microbiota modulates root transcriptional responses and enhances tomato drought resilience
items.abstract: Summary Compost is a promising sustainable alternative to mineral fertilization because it supplies nutrients and organic matter while hosting diverse microbial communities. However, even if its application to plants has been proven to alleviate different biotic and abiotic stresses, it remains unclear whether its benefits arise from its physico-chemical properties, its associated microbiota, or both. In this study, we compared the impact of compost, sterile compost and an NPK treatment providing equivalent macronutrient inputs on tomato plants cv. Micro-Tom. After assessing physiological parameters of the leaves and molecular responses of the roots under optimal conditions, we performed a drought stress experiment under the three fertilization treatments, complementing the analysis with the investigation of substrate water-retention properties. Although all fertilized treatments improved plant performance relative to nutrient-poor soil, RNA sequencing revealed distinct root transcriptional profiles among compost, sterile compost and NPK, with the compost treatment upregulating several pathways related to plant growth and health, such as hormone signaling, nutrient metabolism, and stress responses. When subjected to severe water stress, compost-treated plants retained the highest photosynthetic efficiency and compost showed the highest available water content compared to the other treatments. These findings suggest that compost may enhance tomato drought resilience through combined effects of substrate water availability and compost-associated microbiota.
items.authors: Cipriani, R., Strickler, S. R., Petruzzellis, F., Ghirardello, G., Greggio, L., Zanardi, W., Bonato, T., Baldan, B., Nigris, S.

items.title: Spatial Decoupling of the Endodermal Functions Establishes the Innermost Cortex as the Gravity Sensor in Rice Stems
items.abstract: Gravitropism is a remarkable example of coordinated growth, enabling plants to perceive gravity and generate asymmetric cell expansion that restores organ orientation. In Arabidopsis, gravity sensing in shoots occurs within starch-rich endodermis cells. In rice, however, the stem must accommodate gravitropic bending while preserving integrity of tissues surrounding emerging crown roots, raising the possibility that gravity sensing relies on distinct structural and physiological adaptations. Here, using high-resolution imaging together with auxin-response analyses, we identify a specialized cell layer at the inner boundary of the rice stem cortex, operationally defined by its position adjacent to the lignified endodermis and associated with gravitropic responses. This layer is characterized by circumferentially elongated cells, starch sedimentation, a confined auxin-response domain, and expression of gravity-sensing markers. Following gravistimulation, starch granules realign and the auxin response domain expands asymmetrically within this layer, coinciding with differential growth during stem bending. Our results further indicate that this response depends on polar auxin transport and conserved components of the gravitropic regulatory network. Together, these findings support a model in which gravity sensing and signaling in rice stems are spatially separated from the lignified endodermal barrier. Such tissue organization may represent a developmental adaptation that allows the stem to reconcile barrier integrity with growth flexibility.
items.authors: Kashyap, R., Singh, Z., Kumar, A., Gupta, Y., Kumar, A., Singh, S., Jouannic, S., Bergougnoux, V., Prasad, K., Gantet, P., Yadav, S. R.

items.title: Cortical lacunae, not xylem embolism, drive interspecific differences in freeze-thaw hydraulic dysfunction of conifer fine roots.
items.abstract: Winter snowpack loss exposes fine roots to freeze-thaw cycles at high latitudes and elevations, but the mechanisms of injury and reasons for species differences in vulnerability are not well understood. Motivated by yellow-cedar decline, we evaluated competing mechanisms of freeze-thaw hydraulic dysfunction (xylem embolism and cortical lacunae) and whether root economics strategy predicts susceptibility. We subjected 96 seedlings of four co-occurring Pacific Northwest conifers (mountain hemlock, western hemlock, western redcedar, and yellow-cedar) to seven daily temperature cycles with minima of 3, -3, or -9°C, quantifying xylem and radial conductivity loss, cortical lacunae, and root economics traits. Xylem conductivity loss was low in all species and treatments (mean 11-14%). Yellow-cedar averaged 58% simulated radial conductivity loss at -9°C, with lacunae occupying 20% of cortical area. Hemlocks (with pervasively lignified cortical walls) rarely formed lacunae, whereas cedars (with largely unlignified walls reinforced by phi-thickenings) were more susceptible. More acquisitive roots were more vulnerable, among and within species. Our results indicate that cortical lacunae, not xylem embolism, drive interspecific differences in freeze-thaw hydraulic dysfunction, which was most severe in yellow-cedar. Vulnerability corresponded to cortical wall construction and root economics strategy, providing a mechanistic basis for yellow-cedar's unique susceptibility to snowpack loss.
items.authors: Simovic M, Michaletz ST.

items.title: Comparative transcriptomic responses of tomato to Xanthomonas strains isolated from different hosts.
items.abstract: Bacterial spot disease, caused by several Xanthomonas species, poses a significant threat to tomato and pepper production worldwide. Among these pathogens, Xanthomonas vesicatoria and Xanthomonas euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria have emerged as particularly important pathogens due to their widespread distribution and economic impact. While both pathogens cause similar symptoms, their genetic and pathogenic differences influence infection dynamics. In this study, we conducted a comparative transcriptomic analysis of tomato plants infected with one strain of X. vesicatoria (isolated from tomato) and one of X. euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria (isolated from pepper) to elucidate differential gene expression patterns associated with tomato defense responses. RNA sequencing at 48 hours post-infection revealed a higher number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in response to X. vesicatoria, with significant enrichment in pathways related to cell wall modification, secondary metabolism, and phytohormone signaling. On the other hand, infection with X. euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria induced a more limited transcriptomic response, with upregulation of a lesser number of genes involved in stress response. Key defense-related genes, including pathogenesis-related proteins (PR1, PR2, PR5), chitinases, and peroxidases, were activated in both infections but showed higher expression levels in response to X. vesicatoria. These findings suggest that X. vesicatoria elicits a stronger immune response in tomato plants than X. euvesicatoria pv. euvesicatoria under the conditions tested. This differential response likely reflects distinct interaction strategies employed by these strains during host colonization. Overall, our study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying tomato-Xanthomonas interactions and identifies potential molecular targets for developing bacterial spot-resistant cultivars.
items.authors: Sánchez-Giménez L, Llorens E, Farvardin A, Cubero J, Scalschi L, Vicedo B, Camañes G.

items.title: Combined Bacillus velezensis-Brevibacterium frigoritolerans Biostimulant and Melatonin Improves Salt Tolerance in Maize Seedlings and Is associated with Physiological and Transcriptome-Metabolome Changes.
items.abstract: Salt stress severely limits maize seedling establishment, and microbiology-based biostimulants offer a promising strategy for improving crop performance under salinity. However, whether plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) can complement melatonin (MT) in regulating maize salt responses remains unclear. Here, maize seedlings grown hydroponically under 100 mM NaCl were treated with a mixed PGPR inoculant comprising Bacillus velezensis and Brevibacterium frigoritolerans, foliar MT, or their combination. Physiological traits were measured across eight treatments, and comparative transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses were performed between salt stress alone (S) and the combined treatment (S+R+MT). The combined treatment more effectively restored plant height, root length, biomass, root activity, photosynthetic pigments, proline, soluble sugars, and antioxidant enzyme activities than single treatments, while decreasing malondialdehyde and H2O2 accumulation. Untargeted metabolomics identified 836 differential metabolites, mainly enriched in amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism, the pentose phosphate pathway, nucleotide metabolism, and ABC transporters. Transcriptome analysis identified 7,307 differentially expressed genes enriched in carbon metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, starch and sucrose metabolism, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and MAPK signaling. Integrated analysis indicated that the combined treatment coordinated osmotic adjustment, carbon allocation, glutathione/ascorbate-associated redox buffering, and phenylpropanoid-related defense. These results indicate that co-application of PGPR and MT can improve the salt tolerance of maize seedlings under controlled hydroponic NaCl stress.
items.authors: Li X, Wang C, Feng Q, Qiao Y, Zhang Y.

items.title: Strigolactone analog GR24 modulates hyphal growth, mitochondrial activity, and superoxide accumulation in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Rhizopogon roseolus
items.abstract: Abstract Plant hormone strigolactone (SL) is an important rhizosphere signal that mediate communication between plants and diverse soil organisms. However, the role of SL in ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungi remains largely unexplored, despite ECM fungi representing a major group of plant symbiotic fungi. To address this knowledge gap, we examined the effects of widely used SL analog GR24 with different stereoisomers and concentrations on several ECM fungal species. Deeper investigation on cellular and transcriptional response to GR24 was conducted on Rhizopogon roseolus . The evaluated parameters include fungal growth and branching, mitochondrial activity, superoxide accumulation, Ca 2+ signaling, and gene expression. Our findings reveal that ECM fungal responses to GR24 depend on fungal species, as well as GR24 stereoisomers and concentration. Further analysis on R. roseolus suggested that GR24 enhanced mitochondrial activity and increased mitochondria-associated superoxide accumulation. Based on pharmacological approach, the response of R. roseolus to GR24 required extracellular Ca 2+ influx. Consistent with these morphological and cellular responses, GR24 induce transcriptional response in genes related to cell-wall biosynthesis, mitochondrial respiratory chain, superoxide detoxification, and Ca 2+ signaling. Together, these findings provide novel insight into SL responsiveness in ECM fungi by integrating morphological, cellular, and transcriptional analyses.
items.authors: Pratiwi MN, Nathawan K, Chollada S, Hiroyuki A, Aimi T, Shimomura N.

items.title: An alfalfa MYB71-centered activation-attenuation module fine-tunes redox homeostasis and drought tolerance in Medicago sativa.
items.abstract: Drought severely constrains alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) productivity, yet dissecting drought-response mechanisms in this important perennial forage crop remains challenging because of its highly heterozygous autotetraploid genome, the extended cycle required for stable transformation and regeneration, and the time-consuming evaluation of drought responses in mature plants. Here, we identified MsMYB71, a drought-responsive R2R3-MYB transcription factor, as a positive regulator of drought tolerance in alfalfa. Mechanistically, MsMYB71 directly bound to the promoter of MsPrxQ (peroxiredoxin Q), encoding a chloroplast-associated peroxiredoxin Q, and activated its expression, thereby promoting redox homeostasis under drought stress. In contrast, MsPRL1 (PLEIOTROPIC REGULATORY LOCUS 1, a WD40-repeat protein) and MsCUL4 (Cullin4, a Cullin-family scaffold protein) interacted with MsMYB71 and attenuated its protein accumulation and transcriptional output. To establish the physiological relevance of this regulatory module directly in alfalfa, we generated stable overexpression and RNA interference lines for all four genes. Genetic and physiological analyses showed that MsMYB71 enhanced drought tolerance and restricted excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation. Stable manipulation of MsPrxQ further established its positive role in drought tolerance and antioxidant defense. In contrast, MsPRL1 and MsCUL4 negatively regulated drought tolerance and physically interacted with MsMYB71. Their co-expression reduced MsMYB71 protein accumulation in a proteasome-sensitive manner and attenuated MsMYB71-dependent activation of MsPrxQ, consistent with an MsPRL1/MsCUL4-associated attenuation mechanism. Together, our findings define an MsPRL1/MsCUL4-MsMYB71-MsPrxQ module that couples transcriptional activation with protein-level attenuation to fine-tune redox homeostasis and drought adaptation in alfalfa.
items.authors: Han B, Dong X, Shi C, Mao P, Zhang Y, Zhou Q, Fang L, Liu W, Fu C, Wen J, Liu Z.

items.title: Long-read methylome profiling reveals context-specific epigenetic responses of Brassica napus to Verticillium longisporum.
items.abstract: BackgroundCanola (Brassica napus L.) is a commercially important oilseed crop threatened by Verticillium longisporum, a soil-borne vascular fungal pathogen. While genetic resistance has been widely studied, the role of epigenetic regulation in plant responses to vascular fungal infection remains poorly understood, particularly in polyploid crop species. This study aimed to characterize genome-wide DNA methylation dynamics in B. napus following V. longisporum infection using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing.ResultsONT sequencing enabled direct profiling of DNA methylation in infected and mock-inoculated plants. A total of 824, 267, and 19 differentially methylated windows (DMWs) were identified in CG, CHG, and CHH contexts, respectively. DMWs were distributed across both gene-associated and transposable element regions, with distinct context-specific patterns. Multiple DMWs overlapped genes associated with plant defense, including those involved in receptor-like kinase signaling, oxidative stress responses, calcium signaling, and transcriptional regulation. In addition, intergenic methylation changes proximal to defense-related genes identify candidate regulatory regions that warrant future functional validation.ConclusionsV. longisporum infection was associated with localized and context-dependent changes in DNA methylation in B. napus, with most variation occurring in CG and CHG contexts. The association of DMWs with defense-related genes suggests that DNA methylation may contribute to the regulation of plant responses during vascular fungal infection. These findings provide new insights into epigenetic responses in a complex polyploid crop and establish a foundation for future studies investigating the role of DNA methylation in plant disease responses.
items.authors: Kaur G, Masand M, Stasolla C, Walkowiak S, Chawla H.

items.title: IDENTIFICATION OF CANDIDATE GENES UNDERLYING A NOVEL QTL FOR ROOT LENGTH AND DIAMETER IN BARLEY IN RESPONSE TO SALINITY
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Salinity is a major agricultural problem that decreases growth and yield of crops and is expected to worsen with climate change. Improving salt tolerance through breeding could be facilitated by identification of genetic loci and candidate genes affecting root traits that enhance water and nutrient uptake while limiting accumulation of toxic ions. In this study, a Clipper x Sahara 3771 doubled haploid (DH) barley mapping population was screened for root growth responses to saline conditions in a controlled environment. Quantitative trait loci (QTLs) were mapped for root traits including seminal root length, root diameter and root potassium. Major QTLs affecting seminal root length and average root diameter were detected in the distal region of the short arm of chromosome 2H, indicating that this region is a key determinant of root architecture under both control and saline conditions. The linkage map was improved by using newly designed assays for SNPs on chromosome 2H and a 2.5-Mb interval was identified for investigation of candidate genes. Bulked segregant RNA sequencing (BSR-Seq) of contrasting salt-tolerant and salt-sensitive DH lines identified differentially expressed genes associated with root growth maintenance and ion homeostasis in root tips. These findings identify specific region on chromosome 2H as a major genomic region affecting barley root architecture, especially under saline conditions, and identify differentially expressed candidate genes in that region.
items.authors: Mather, D., Situmorang, A., Brien, C., Shelden, M.

items.title: Quantification of spatial heterogeneity of different chlorophyll fluorescence parameters over tomato leaf areas affected by Cd2+ stress.
items.abstract: Cadmium impairs plant growth by inducing oxidative damage through excessive ROS production. Sulfur and nitrogen supplementation can affect Cd mobility, uptake, and toxicity. This study quantifies the spatial heterogeneity of Cd-induced photochemical limitation in Solanum lycopersicum leaves using chlorophyll fluorescence imaging, and examines Cd2+ distribution in roots, stems, and leaves of hydroponic plants treated with ammonium sulfate. We assessed four treatments: control, ammonium sulfate (5 mM), cadmium (100 µM CdCl2), and their combination, using fluorescence imaging, the JIP-test, and polarography. Cd stress was intrinsically heterogeneous within single leaves, with the strongest PSII inhibition along vascular tissue and leaf tips. Contrary to expectations, ammonium sulfate failed to mitigate Cd toxicity, suggesting an adverse ammonium-Cd interaction. OJIP analysis revealed severe oxygen-evolving complex damage under combined treatment, marked by prominent K- and L-bands. These findings highlight the localised nature of Cd stress and reveal responses missed by whole-leaf measurements.
items.authors: Giordano D, Saadati A, Ashrafi AM, Richtera L, Barták M.

items.title: S -nitrosoglutathione reductase acts as a mitophagy receptor to control mitochondrial quality in plants
items.abstract: Mitochondria are central for cellular energy metabolism, and their quality is warranted by multiple mechanisms, including mitophagy, a process of selectively removing damaged, aged, or excess mitochondria. However, the regulatory mechanism of mitophagy remains elusive in plants. Here, we report that Arabidopsis S -nitrosoglutathione reductase 1 (GSNOR1), an enzyme that has long been known to degrade S -nitrosoglutathione, interacts with the outer mitochondrial membrane protein Voltage-Dependent Anion Channel 3 (VDAC3) to mediate mitophagy. GSNOR1 translocates to depolarized mitochondria, binds to VDAC3, and interacts with Autophagy-related 8 (ATG8) via its ATG8-interacting motifs, thereby engulfing damaged mitochondria in autophagosomes for mitophagic degradation. Mutations in GSNOR1 or VDAC3 cause the accumulation of misshapen mitochondria and hypersensitivity to mitochondrial stress. We propose that GSNOR1 acts as a cargo receptor interacting with VDAC3 and ATG8 to target depolarized mitochondria to mitophagy, thereby regulating cellular homeostasis.
items.authors: Lin, H., Guo, H., Wu, R., Wang, W., Jia, P.-F., Sun, S., Bie, R., Li, H.-J., Yang, W.-C., Zuo, J.

items.title: An in vivo fluorescence imaging approach for real-time monitoring of ROS-associated oxidative responses in harvested lettuce leaves.
items.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) play a key role in postharvest quality and senescence of fresh produce, yet their real-time monitoring in intact tissues remains challenging. In this study, we developed and evaluated an in vivo fluorescence imaging approach for monitoring ROS dynamics in whole harvested lettuce leaves using the ROS-sensitive probe 2', 7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (H2DCF-DA). The stability of the probe and the sensitivity of the imaging system were first assessed under a tissue-free condition. Subsequently, the method was applied to whole lettuce leaves subjected to exogenous hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) or ultraviolet-C (UV-C) irradiations at doses of 0.85, 1.71 and 3.42 kj/m2. A strong and stable fluorescence signal in the presence of H2O2 under tissue-free conditions was observed, confirming probe reactivity and the system detection sensitivity. Exogenous H2O2 application in whole lettuce leaves, resulted in a progressive increase in ROS-associated fluorescence, whereas UV-C irradiation induced a rapid and dose-dependent fluorescence response followed by a gradual decline, indicative of a transient oxidative burst and subsequent redox regulation. These findings demonstrate that in vivo fluorescence imaging is a sensitive and non-invasive tool for real-time monitoring of ROS in harvested produce. This approach offers new perspectives for investigating oxidative stress dynamics relevant to postharvest quality management of fruits and vegetables.
items.authors: Bata Gouda MH, Cordella CBY, Duarte-Sierra A.

items.title: Ambivalent roles of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay in heat stress tolerance
items.abstract: RNA homeostasis is essential for gene regulation and cellular survival; however, how RNA degradation pathways contribute to stress adaptation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) in regulating heat stress (HS) memory in a long-term acquired thermotolerance assay. NMD-deficient Arabidopsis thaliana mutants upf1-5 and upf3-1 exhibited a biphasic phenotype: they displayed transiently elevated heat tolerance during early recovery but became more sensitive to heat during late recovery. Genetic analysis of upf3;hsfa2 and upf3;hsfa3 double mutants demonstrated that the early heat tolerance occurs independently of both HsfA2 and HsfA3 HS- memory transcription factors. Under non-treated conditions, the upf3-1 transcriptome exhibited baseline priming of heat-shock responsive transcripts, likely accounting for the initial heat tolerance. Further transcriptome profiling revealed that upf3-1 mutants exhibited reduced levels of the functional HsfA2 isoform ( HsfA2-I ) and attenuated expression of the HsfA2- dependent thermomemory regulon following the triggering stress. NMD deficiency also upregulated immune-response genes while repressing developmental and cell-wall-associated pathways. Together, impaired HsfA2-dependent thermomemory and a compromised growth– defense balance underlies the late heat sensitivity of NMD-deficient plants. Overall, NMD acts as a dual-action post-transcriptional regulator that coordinates the transition from stress response to growth resumption. Highlight statement Arabidopsis NMD Mutants Exhibit a Biphasic Heat Stress Response, with Early HsfA2/A3-Independent Tolerance and Late HsfA2-Dependent Sensitivity.
items.authors: Abbas, S. H., Szaker, H. M., Darko, E., Eros, T., Silhavy, D., Csorba, T.

items.title: TaMYB39 positively regulates salt tolerance in wheat seedlings.
items.abstract: Salt stress severely restricts wheat growth and productivity, yet the regulatory mechanisms governing the abundance and activity of stress-responsive transcription factors remain incompletely understood. In this study, we characterized the wheat MYB transcription factor TaMYB39 and investigated its role in salt tolerance and protein stability. TaMYB39 expression was rapidly induced by NaCl treatment, and the protein was predominantly localized in the nucleus. Transgenic wheat lines overexpressing TaMYB39 exhibited improved growth and greater dry weight under salt stress, whereas RNAi lines showed increased sensitivity. TaMYB39 overexpression was associated with reduced Na⁺ accumulation, enhanced K⁺ retention, a lower Na⁺/K⁺ ratio, increased proline accumulation, and reduced membrane damage. The overexpression lines also accumulated less H2O2 and O2- and exhibited higher SOD, POD, and CAT activities, consistent with enhanced antioxidant capacity. Yeast two-hybrid screening identified the bZIP transcription factor TabZIP27 as a TaMYB39-interacting protein, and this interaction was confirmed by pairwise Y2H, BiFC, GST pull-down, and Co-IP assays. Salt treatment enhanced the TaMYB39-TabZIP27 interaction. Cell-free degradation and CHX chase assays further showed that TabZIP27 delayed TaMYB39 degradation, whereas MG132 treatment attenuated the decline in TaMYB39 abundance, supporting the involvement of the 26S proteasome pathway in TaMYB39 turnover. Collectively, these findings identify TaMYB39 as a positive regulator of salt tolerance in wheat and suggest that its protein stability is modulated through interaction with TabZIP27 under salt stress.
items.authors: Zhang G, Wang K, Guo M, He M, Tan Y, Shi Y, Si C, Fan J, Yan M.

items.title: Phosphoprotein Phosphatases (PPP), Important Molecular Switchers in Plant Cell and Environment Responses.
items.abstract: Protein phosphatases, the executors of protein dephosphorylation, play indispensable roles in plant growth, development, and stress adaptation. This review summarizes the classification and biological functions of plant protein phosphatases, with a specific focus on the phosphoprotein phosphatase (PPP) family. By forming dynamic holoenzyme complexes with diverse regulatory subunits, PPP precisely controls vital cellular processes such as hormone signalling pathways, cell division, and light responses. Recent studies highlight the critical involvement of PPP in immune defence and abiotic stress adaptation, including drought and salt tolerance. Although PP1 and PP2A are extensively studied in non-plant systems, functionally dissecting PPP in plants remains an essential frontier, particularly in elucidating isoform-specific functions, mapping regulatory subunit-substrate-kinase networks, and decoding post-translational modifications. Looking forward, integrating phosphoproteomics with advanced toolkits, such as TurboID proximity labelling, AP-MS, substrate-trapping mutants, as well as single-cell and spatial omics, alongside bioinformatics, will be pivotal in overcoming these challenges. Ultimately, engineering regulatory subunit-PPP-substrate modules for crop improvement. Given that protein phosphatases are emerging as a pivotal regulatory hub for balancing the growth-defence trade-off, unravelling their multifaceted roles will simultaneously advance fundamental plant biology and drive innovations in precision breeding.
items.authors: Qin Q, Shi W, Hou S.

items.title: Integrative transcriptome meta-analysis distinguishes compatibility and incompatibility in rice-Xanthomonas interaction.
items.abstract: Diseases caused by the Xanthomonas oryzae pathovars are important constraints for global rice productivity. Despite being a well-studied pathosystem, the transcriptional mechanisms distinguishing resistance from susceptibility remain incompletely understood. Here, we present a systems-level meta-analysis of more than a hundred publicly available rice-Xanthomonas transcriptome datasets. Using appropriate analysis pipelines, stringent filtering criteria and metadata integration, we identified rice functions that distinguish disease resistance and susceptibility with temporal resolution. Compatible interactions were characterized by early activation of abscisic-acid biosynthetic and signaling genes, and extensive transcriptional plasticity associated with susceptibility gene activation. In contrast, incompatible interactions displayed a restrained transcriptome reprogramming, enrichment of phenylpropanoid and aromatic-amino-acid biosynthetic pathways, and enrichment of an AP2/ERF-GCC-box regulatory module. Transient over-expression of three conserved infection-responsive genes, OsJAZ11, OsSYP131b, and OsMYB45, modestly enhanced defense gene expression and reduced lesion length caused by X. oryzae pv. oryzae in rice leaves, thus providing a proof-of-concept relevance of the candidates to rice-Xoo interaction. We also developed RiceXtra, an openly available database hosting the analyzed data (http://tdb.ccmb.res.in/RiceXtra), for exploring gene expression patterns during rice-Xanthomonas interactions. Overall, our study proposes a mechanistic framework connecting hormonal signalling and transcriptional plasticity with disease outcome, offering a foundation for engineering durable disease resistance.
items.authors: Cg G, Malukani KK, Gaur N, M S, Patel HK, Sonti RV.

items.title: Rhg1-mediated selective autophagy degrades the nematode effector HgGID to increase soybean cyst nematode resistance.
items.abstract: Plant-parasitic nematodes are sophisticated metazoan pathogens that deploy complex, animal-like effector repertoires to manipulate host cellular machinery. The Rhg1 locus drives the primary resistance against soybean cyst nematode (Heterodera glycines), yet the mechanism by which its encoded atypical Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor Attachment Protein 18 (SNAP18) proteins restrict this evolutionarily advanced pathogen remains a long-standing enigma. Here, we reveal that Rhg1-mediated resistance operates as a suicide-bait strategy that converts a nematode virulence factor into a selective-autophagic trap. TurboID proximity labeling identified HgGID (glucose-induced degradation), a secreted nematode effector that physically associates with SNAP18 and co-enriches ubiquitin-proteasome components and SNARE-associated factors, consistent with a virulence strategy that engages host trafficking machinery during syncytium formation. Notably, the Rhg1-encoded atypical SNAP18 variant subverts this virulence strategy. We show that HgGID binds all 3 SNAP18 variants, whereas the resistance-associated SNAP18LC/HC variants favor increased dynamic accessibility of the HgGID AIM and promote its ATG8-dependent selective degradation. Ultimately, this targeted autophagic clearance efficiently neutralizes the virulence function of HgGID, establishing a novel paradigm for plant immunity against metazoan pathogens. Our findings uncover a molecular arms race where the host repurposes its vesicle transport machinery into an immune trap, highlighting the central role of selective autophagy in determining the outcome of host-metazoan interactions.
items.authors: Wang L, Chen L, Wu W, Jin Y, Liu Q, Xie L, Song F, Liang Y, Shen XX, Han S.

items.title: Four universal modules and their combinations for decoding amplitude and frequency of Ca2+ signals in plants.
items.abstract: Calcium signals are fundamental for plants and play crucial roles in developmental processes and in rapid responses to environmental stimuli and stress factors. Nevertheless, the mechanisms underlying the decoding of calcium signals in plants are still largely unclear. We have addressed the question of Ca2+ signal decoding in a bottom-up modelling approach starting with the thermodynamics of Ca2+ binding to EF hands (EF: Glutamic acid-Phenylalanine) in Ca2+-binding proteins (CBPs). On this basis, we identified four universal, fundamental Ca2+ decoding modules, in which a CBP modulates the activity of a target protein (TP). Representatives of these basic modules are omnipresent in plant cells. Their Ca2+ dependent properties are mainly determined by the interaction of the CBP with the TP rather than the Ca2+-binding properties of the EF hands. Combinations of the modules generated complexes that are also observed in plants, which decode not only the amplitude but also the frequency of Ca2+ signals by setting specific 'frequency islands' in which a TP is active. The modelling approach presented here addresses the decoding of Ca2+ signals from the microscopic to the systemic level and could help to find the 'Rosetta Stone' for Ca2+ signalling in plants.
items.authors: Vergara-Valladares F, Rubio-Meléndez ME, Charpentier M, Michard E, Dreyer I.

items.title: Spatiotemporal transcriptome atlas of water lily floral organogenesis provides insight to the evolutionary origin of petals in basal angiosperms.
items.abstract: BackgroundPetals are a key evolutionary innovation of flowers that reshape plant-pollinator interactions and contribute to the dominance of angiosperms in terrestrial ecosystems. However, their evolutionary origin remains debated as previous studies have largely relied on morphological inferences with limited spatially resolved molecular evidence during floral organogenesis.ResultsHere we employ spatial transcriptome sequencing on developing floral buds of the basal angiosperm Nymphaea colorata to dissect the potential gene regulatory landscape underlying petal formation. Our analyses reveal an unexpected hierarchical structure of four meristematic cell groups that persist at the floral base until carpel formation, displaying a gradient of decreasing meristematic potential along the proximal-distal axis. Among them, one group gives rise to stamens and petals (inner tepals). Developmental trajectory reconstruction further uncovers successive cell-fate transitions from stamen primordium to developing petals. These transitions are driven by quantitative variation in MADS-box tetramers composition that gradually reduces the reproductive identity of outer-whorl floral organs. Spatial mapping of developmental regulatory modules involving thousands of tissue-preferentially expressed genes demonstrate that petal morphogenesis integrates additional leaf-like genetic programs, ultimately distinguishing petals from stamens.ConclusionsTogether, these results uncover the evolutionary derivation of petals from reproductive organs through recruitment of ancestral regulatory networks established before seed plants, providing new insights into the developmental basis and evolutionary innovation of petaloid organs in flowering plants.
items.authors: Liu C, Wang G, Cao B, Li Y, Chen Y, Guo C, Qi J.

items.title: CmALDH2B7 and CmALDH7B4 positively regulate the osmotic stress tolerance in melon (Cucumis melo L.).
items.abstract: Aldehyde dehydrogenases (ALDHs) play critical roles in detoxifying reactive aldehydes and maintaining cellular redox homeostasis under stress conditions. In this study, 17 ALDH genes were identified in melon (Cucumis melo L.). Most CmALDH genes harbor multiple cis-regulatory elements associated with abiotic stress responses and hormone signaling, implicating their roles in environmental adaptation. Subsequently, CmALDH2B7 and CmALDH7B4 were selected for further expression and functional analyses. Both CmALDH2B7 and CmALDH7B4 were highly expressed in flowers, flower buds, and roots, and were strongly induced by osmotic stress. Overexpression of CmALDH2B7 or CmALDH7B4 enhanced the osmotic stress resistance of Arabidopsis plants, while silencing of either gene compromised the osmotic stress tolerance of melon seedlings, as evidenced by accelerated wilting, elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation, and reduced activities of catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and peroxidase (POD). Protein interaction assays revealed that CmALDH2B7 directly interacts with the catalase CmCAT1, whereas CmALDH7B4 does not. This study provides a foundation for understanding the functional diversification of the ALDH superfamily and identifies promising targets for improving drought stress tolerance in melon.
items.authors: Zhu K, Yang H, Zhou S, Yan R, Du J, Gao H, Zhao W.
items.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

items.title: Overexpression of REMORIN1.2 affects salt signaling and tolerance in Arabidopsis.
items.abstract: Salinity is among the most detrimental environmental plant stressors hampering growth, development and immunity. Its impact is increasing due to intensive agricultural practices and climate change. The molecular components linked to the early cellular and molecular events triggered by salt are mostly unknown. Here we show that genes encoding for members of the REMORIN proteins family exhibit dynamic temporal regulation following salt perception. Analogously to pattern-triggered immune signaling, we observed that salt rapidly induces the reorganization of REMORIN1.2 (REM1.2) into plasma membrane nanodomains which colocalize with the actin-nucleating protein FORMIN 6. Overexpression of REM1.2 inhibits early signaling and late cell morphological responses to salt, defects which correlated with an increase in salt sensitivity. Our findings connect early salt-triggered signaling events to changes in cell architecture and root resilience and describe FORMIN-containing REMORIN nanodomains as a convergent articulation point in biotic and abiotic signaling pathways.

items.title: Author Correction: Pathogen-induced condensation of the guard cell RNA-binding protein SAIR1 fine-tunes translation for immunity.

items.title: Exogenous Kaempferol Application Enhances Salt Tolerance Over Quercetin in Apocynum pictum Seedlings: An Integrated Multi-Level Analysis.
items.abstract: Salinity stress limits plant growth by disrupting water uptake and inducing ion toxicity. Natural bioactive molecules, including flavonols, have gained attention for their potential to enhance abiotic stress tolerance. This study aimed to compare the effects of exogenous kaempferol (200 μmol L-1) and quercetin (25 μmol L-1) on growth and stress mitigation in Apocynum pictum seedlings under salt stress. Although both flavonoids alleviate salt stress in various species, their regulatory roles in A. pictum remain unclear. Both compounds significantly alleviated salt-induced growth inhibition, with kaempferol showing stronger effects on plant height, leaf number, leaf length, and root length. Ultrastructural analysis revealed distinct protective strategies: kaempferol enhanced cellular structural stability by preserving root cell integrity and promoting cell wall thickening, whereas quercetin maintained mitochondrial integrity and abundance. Kaempferol treatment also resulted in higher superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, soluble protein accumulation, and photosynthetic pigment levels compared to quercetin. Transcriptomic profiling uncovered distinct regulatory mechanisms: quercetin primarily activated the ABC transporter pathway for ion homeostasis, whereas kaempferol markedly stimulated the flavonoid biosynthesis pathway by upregulating key structural genes (CHS, CHI, F3H, F3'H, LAR), suggesting enhanced flavonoid accumulation. Collectively, kaempferol and quercetin employ different yet effective strategies to confer salt tolerance in A. pictum. This study highlights the potential of exogenous kaempferol as a biosafe strategy to enhance plant stress tolerance in agricultural systems.
items.authors: Dong X, Buttar ZA, Ji Y, Cong R, Shi L, Zhao B, Jiang L.

items.title: BcPHT1;9 mediates phosphate uptake and modulates root architecture in flowering Chinese cabbage.
items.abstract: BackgroundPhosphorus (P) is an essential macronutrient for plant growth and development. The absorption and transport of phosphate in plants rely on phosphate transporter-encoded proteins, named PHT1 transporters. Flowering Chinese cabbage is an important vegetable crop, while the molecular mechanisms underlying PHT1-mediated phosphate adaptation to low-phosphate stress remain poorly understood in this species.ResultsIn this study, we identified 13 PHT1 transporter proteins in flowering Chinese cabbage, BcPHT1;9 was predominantly expressed in the roots and localized to the plasma membrane. Overexpression of BcPHT1;9 significantly increased total root length, surface area, and phosphorus content under low-phosphate stress, whereas silencing suppressed these traits. BcPHT1;9 thus coordinately regulates Pi uptake, phosphate homeostasis, and root architectural adaptation to sustain balanced phosphorus nutrition under phosphate-deficient conditions.ConclusionBcPHT1;9 positively enhances low-Pi tolerance by coordinating phosphate uptake and root architecture in flowering Chinese cabbage.
items.authors: Yang W, Xue Y, Anwar A, Hu C, Zhang M, Chen C, Wang J, Song S.

items.title: A multidimensional “omics” approach reveals biased signaling through flg22- and UDP-glucose-induced, AtRGS1-driven signaling circuits
items.abstract: Abstract Different cellular inputs into a central signaling core elicit different outputs in a process called biased signaling. Often this occurs by imprinting the signaling core with a phosphorylation bar code, functionally analogous to a microprocessor. The bacterial peptide flg22 and UDP-glucose both utilize a heterologous G protein core that contains a 7-transmembrane RGS protein, AtRGS1, to mediate changes differentially in plant defense and growth. Both flg22 and UDP-glucose launch rapid endocytosis of AtRGS1 at the plasma membrane but the destination and route are signal specific. flg22 directs plasma membrane AtRGS1 to the nucleus followed by different gene expression profiles. UDP-glucose does not direct AtRGS1 to the nucleus and does not elicit transcriptional reprogramming. Instead, UDP-glucose causes a massive, time-dependent restructuring of the G protein complex that likely traffics to the endosomal compartment. Associated with these two outcomes are phosphorylation bar codes that correlate with different patterns of AtRGS1-associated partners over time.
items.authors: Walley J, Li Z, Simoni E, Yang J, Montes C, Jones A.

items.title: Why be deciduous in a tropical savanna climate? Insights from leaf deployment, stem growth and sap flow dynamics.
items.abstract: Savannas are ecosystems with hot and wet summers and warm and dry winters. How and why savanna trees partition their physiological activity through this seasonal cycle is unknown; yet it is important to understand this temporal partitioning in order to anticipate how anthropogenic climatic change will impact the functioning of savannas. In a South African savanna ecosystem, we examined the temporal pattern of leaf deployment, sap flow and stem increment phenology over three growing seasons for six species. We found that although the phenologies varied between years, there was a high degree of temporal overlap in leaf, sap flow and stem increment phenology between the six study species. Further, we found that a surprisingly large proportion of days on which the measured soil water potential was sufficient for physiological activity remained unused. Although our data are consistent with convergent selection for deciduousness, the unused soil water niche we detected suggests that climate should select for evergreen strategies. Possible explanations for the dominance of deciduousness in these savannas relate to the costs of leaf construction coupled with the risk of leaf destruction due to fire and/or foliovory.
items.authors: Higgins SI, Wigley BJ, Coetsee C, Pallett NCM, February EC.

items.title: Bringing seed barriers into focus: Optimized clearing and histological staining.
items.abstract: Plant reproduction relies on tightly coordinated developmental programs that integrate environmental and endogenous signals. Within seeds, lipid-based extracellular polymers such as cutin and suberin are deposited at defined apoplastic interfaces, where they function as selectively permeable barriers. These structures are actively remodeled by hormonal and metabolic cues to regulate hydration, nutrient exchange, and stress responses. Although the genetic and biochemical pathways underlying these barriers are increasingly well understood, their spatial organization and developmental dynamics remain difficult to investigate because they are embedded within optically dense and multilayered tissues. Existing clearing approaches have substantially improved visualization of internal seed structures, yet systematic whole-mount imaging of multiple lipid-based barriers across development, particularly in combination with fluorescent reporters, remains challenging. To address this, we developed an optimized pipeline that enables rapid and efficient seed tissue clearing and selective visualization of polyaliphatic barriers across four key seed interfaces: the seed surface, seed coat suberin, cuticle at the endosperm/seed coat boundary, and embryo surface cuticle. The method preserves the spatial context of these barriers within intact seeds and enables their co-visualization with fluorescence-based marker lines. Using a common whole-mount imaging framework across successive developmental stages, we follow changes in the spatial organization of distinct barrier domains. The approach is also applicable to more complex seeds, such as those of Camelina sativa, and can be extended to other anatomically complex plant organs by combining the clearing and staining workflow with vibratome sectioning.
items.authors: Ramamonjy FN, Piccinini L, Loaiza VR, Meng H, Ursache R.
items.journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology

items.title: Chloroplast movements in siphonous macroalgae in response to high light and grazing.
items.abstract: Fast cytoplasmic streaming enables extensive chloroplast movements in the giant cells of unicellular, siphonous macroalgae. We studied chloroplast movements by light microscopy, macro-photography and pulse modulated chlorophyll a fluorescence in two such algae: Dasycladalean Acetabularia acetabulum and Bryopsidales Bryopsis sp.. Chemical inhibitors of actin polymerization and microtubule assembly were used to confirm that the observed effects were controlled by the cytoskeleton. Macro-imaging suggest that A. acetabulum responded to high light by reversible chloroplast aggregation, and inhibition of the movements led to increased Photosystem II photoinhibition, probed by the fluorescence parameter FV/FM. In A. acetabulum, wounding caused by cutting or feeding by the sap-sucking sea slug Elysia timida triggered appearance of darker and lighter cell regions, presumably chloroplast aggregation, within minutes of incurring damage. Addition of media collected from vicinity of cut algae was sufficient to induce these aggregations in intact algae, suggesting that water-borne cues or signals triggered the response. On the other hand, only minimal cytoplasmic changes were observed in Bryopsis sp. in response to high light or cutting. The relevance of chloroplast movements in protection against abiotic and biotic stressors in A. acetabulum, and the potential reasons behind the different defence strategies of the algae, are discussed.
items.authors: Mattila H, Lopes P, Havurinne V, Goessling JW, Cartaxana P, Cruz S.

items.title: Exogenous melatonin enhances drought tolerance and secondary-metabolite accumulation in Paeonia ostii 'Fengdan' in association with improved PSI-PSII photochemical coordination.
items.abstract: Drought limits the growth of Paeonia ostii 'Fengdan'. While melatonin (MT) is known to enhance general drought tolerance, its association with Photosystem I-Photosystem II (PSI-PSII) photochemical coordination and secondary-metabolite accumulation in P. ostii remains unclear. We foliar-sprayed potted plants under simulated drought with 0, 50, 100, 200, and 400 μmol(MT) L-1. Drought induced severe oxidative damage, impaired photosynthesis, and disrupted photochemical coordination between PSI and PSII. Among all treatments, 100 μmol(MT) L-1 proved the most effective. It coincided with reduced reactive oxygen species and membrane damage, alongside increased antioxidants, osmolytes, and PSI/PSII performance. Furthermore, compared to drought alone, 100 μmol(MT) L-1 treatment increased the root-bark contents of total flavonoids, total phenolics, gallic acid, catechin, albiflorin, paeoniflorin, benzoic acid, and paeonol by 48.1, 36.1, 17.7, 69.4, 69.9, 24.1, 7.7, and 22.7%, respectively. Thus, 100 μmol(MT) L-1 alleviated drought-induced physiological damage and increased selected secondary-metabolite contents in P. ostii.
items.authors: Zhang LX, Zhang B, Sun YM, Zhao XL, Wang Z, Zhang QM, Zhao KK, Li XF, Hou XG, Chang QS.

items.title: The chloroplast-localised transporter RETICULATA controls palisade mesophyll cell division and expansion
items.abstract: Plant leaves contain extensive intercellular air spaces, which contribute to photosynthetic capacity and water use efficiency in different environments. Despite this importance, the developmental mechanisms that control leaf air space patterning are poorly understood. For over 20 years it has been known that plants with disrupted chloroplast biogenesis and metabolism have increased intercellular air spaces, but the underlying molecular mechanism is unknown. Here, we characterise leaf air space morphogenesis in mutants of the chloroplast amino acid transporter RETICULATA (RE), which has enlarged air spaces. We show that the reticulata-6 (re-6) loss of function mutant exhibits increased air space expansion specifically in the palisade, and not the spongy, mesophyll. We also show that RE does not regulate air space patterning via programmed cell death, via a change in stomatal density or a change in cell identity of the mesophyll tissue. Instead, we quantify mesophyll cell morphology and division rates to show that RE acts by promoting early palisade cell division and suppressing later cell expansion. Overall, we show that RE specifically regulated palisade mesophyll morphogenesis and air space patterning and hypothesise that chloroplasts may act to regulate air space patterning in the palisade mesophyll in response to light.
items.authors: Locke Bevia, E. A., Aldorino, E., Fitzsimons, J. M., Dillon, J. C., Whitewoods, C. D.

items.title: An orphan LuxR regulator controls plant developmental reprogramming during interaction with Novosphingobium resinovorum HR1a
items.abstract: Rhizoremediation depends on productive plant/pollutant-degrading microorganism interactions, yet the bacterial regulatory mechanisms that shape host responses remain poorly understood. We investigated the role of the previously uncharacterized orphan LuxR874 from the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) degrading bacterium Novosphingobium resinovorum HR1a, in the modulation of plant physiology. Bacterial transcriptomics revealed that LuxR874 controls the expression of genes associated with aromatic and sugar metabolism, and acylCoA related functions. Inactivation of luxR874 altered bacterial responses without affecting root colonization, suggesting that this regulator contributes to the physiological state required to elicit host responses. In gnotobiotic systems, HR1a induced a root phenotype characterized by reduced primary root elongation, increased root thickness, and enhanced root hair formation. These alterations were attenuated in the luxR874 mutant and restored by complementation despite similar colonization levels among strains. Plant RNA-seq analyses revealed extensive host transcriptional reprogramming, including activation of developmental regulators, hormone associated pathways, cell wall remodeling genes, and oxidative stress responses. In contrast, plants inoculated with the luxR874 mutant displayed a weaker transcriptional response resembling the non-inoculated state. Functional analyses supported LuxR874-dependent activation of reactive oxygen species and ethylene related pathways. Our results reveal an unexpected role for an orphan LuxR regulator in coordinating multi-level responses during a rhizoremediation-relevant plant microbe interaction.
items.authors: Molina, L., Hurtado, I., Udaondo, Z., Segura, A.

items.title: scPCIP: cross-species annotation of plant cell types with conserved gene programs
items.abstract: Single-cell atlases now cover many plant species and organs, yet their cell types are still annotated with marker genes that often fail to transfer between species. Here we show that plant cell identities are captured by gene programs conserved across species. We learned programs for root, leaf, flower and seed cell types on ortholog groups from 112,905 author-labelled cells and implemented them in scPCIP, which annotates cells of species absent from training without a reference. Across 26 held-out datasets, scPCIP outperformed marker-based and plant deep-learning methods, matched supervised classifiers trained on the same atlas and transferred, at lower accuracy, to an independent study; its programs followed tissue position in spatial transcriptomes. The conserved core of each program separated cell types better than its periphery in all 11 held-out species, whereas most species-specific markers turned over. Across organs, leaf bundle-sheath cells carried a root endodermis program in 8 of 12 studies.

items.title: MoALE1, an ART-like effector, contributes to rice blast virulence through host immune suppression
items.abstract: Rice blast, caused by the hemibiotrophic fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, is one of the most destructive diseases affecting rice production worldwide. During infection, M. oryzae secretes effector proteins that suppress host immunity and facilitate colonization. Here, we characterized MoALE1, a predicted effector that is structurally similar to members of the heat-labile enterotoxin/cholera toxin family. Using a yeast secretion trap assay, we demonstrated that MoALE1 contains a functional signal peptide. A MoALE1-GFP fusion localized to the biotrophic interfacial complex, indicating that MoALE1 is a cytoplasmic effector. Expression analyses revealed that MoALE1 is expressed during biotrophy, from 16 to 48 h post-inoculation. Transient expression in Nicotiana benthamiana showed that MoALE1 suppresses BAX-mediated cell death, suggesting a role in host immune suppression. To investigate its contribution to pathogenicity, a{Delta} moale1 mutant was generated and evaluated in rice infection assays. Deletion of MoALE1 significantly reduced disease severity but did not affect fungal growth, stress tolerance, sporulation, appressorium development, host penetration, or early invasive growth. In contrast, infection by the {Delta}moale1 mutant resulted in enhanced host H2O2 accumulation and increased expression of ROS-associated defense genes. Together, these findings identify MoALE1 as a biotrophy-associated cytoplasmic effector that promotes rice blast pathogenicity by suppressing host immune responses and provide new insight into the function of ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART)-like effector candidates in M. oryzae .
items.authors: Kalicharan, R. E., Payne, N., Tagala, I., Pawlowski, K., Fernandez, J.

items.title: The bHLH121-CAT2 module maintains root tip redox homeostasis to confer salt tolerance additively with the SOS pathway in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: Soil salinity inhibits plant growth, in part, by restricting the availability of essential mineral nutrients such as iron (Fe). Although Fe deficiency frequently coincides with salt stress in the field, the molecular mechanisms integrating Fe homeostasis with salt tolerance remain largely unknown. Here, we identify the Fe deficiency response regulator bHLH121 as a key coordinator of salt tolerance in Arabidopsis. Loss-of-function mutants of bHLH121 exhibit pronounced hypersensitivity to salt stress, with severely impaired primary root elongation and reduced seedling biomass. Transcriptomic and histochemical analyses reveal that bHLH121 is required to maintain reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis specifically in root tips under salt stress. We further demonstrate that CATALASE 2 (CAT2) is a direct downstream target of bHLH121, and that CAT2 overexpression fully rescues the salt hypersensitivity of the bhlh121 mutant. Importantly, this bHLH121-CAT2 module operates independently of the classical SOS pathway, as sos2 bhlh121 double mutants display additive salt sensitivity. Together, our findings uncover a novel regulatory module in which bHLH121 governs root tip redox homeostasis through CAT2 to confer salt tolerance, providing a direct mechanistic link between the Fe regulatory network and abiotic stress resilience in plants.
