items.title: Rapid Electro-optic Two-photon Bessel Light Sheet Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging for Tissue Volume Interrogation
items.abstract: We report a two-photon light sheet electro-optic fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (TPLS-EO-FLIM) technique based on an electro-optic (EO) modulation detection module. Scanning two-photon Bessel light sheet excitation was used to achieve in-depth volumetric imaging. The low cross-section of multiphoton excitation requires high detection efficiency, and electro-optic detection enables fast wide-field FLIM with a scientific complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (sCMOS) detector. Phototoxicity is minimized by utilizing signal from the entire illuminated sample area in a wide field camera exposure, and time-resolved volume acquisitions are feasible in minutes, with cross-sectional field of view and light sheet length over 300 microns. The method has sub-nanosecond lifetime resolution and is capable of accurate FLIM images in 10 ms exposures with as low as a few hundred photons per pixel. The technique was demonstrated through volumetric FLIM of a green fluorescent protein (GFP) labeled zebrafish embryo heart, of multi-fluorescent protein (multi-FP) labeled plant root structures and of dynamic cardiac cycles in live zebrafish embryos. For the latter, we recorded the cardiac cycle dynamics of a zebrafish embryo at 50 frames per second and measured biomechanical parameters such as heart rate, ventricle/atrium areas, atrioventricular valve dynamics, and fractional area change. Taken together, these studies show the capability of the system for rapid, high resolution, and functional imaging in diverse biological contexts.

items.title: Evolution of Vesicle Shape Parameters Based on A Deep-Learning Based Image Analysis Framework Over Extended Time Periods
items.abstract: A precise analysis of shape instabilities in cell-sized membrane compartments requires thorough quantification of the shape dynamics of individual components over extended periods. Herein, we have used phase-contrast microscopy to image giant unilamellar membrane vesicles (GUVs), which are widely used as model systems for cellular structures. GUVs were prepared in the fluid lamellar phase of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine with and without cholesterol dissolved within a potato starch solution. The morphological changes and budding dynamics of individual GUVs with different chemical compositions were quantified using a deep-learning based image analysis framework over extended time periods, by using phase-contrast micrographs as input data. This automated framework integrates contour-based detection of the mother vesicle with precise segmentation of daughter compartments, thereby enabling explicit identification and tracking of mother and daughter vesicles at high temporal resolution. These findings further facilitate the measurement of the temporal evolution of vesicle morphometrics including area, and local membrane curvature during budding, that can be used as an input to develop computational models aimed at elucidating curvature-driven membrane remodeling in complex soft materials.

items.title: Secondary growth in the tomato stem is suppressed by the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3
items.abstract: Herbaceous eudicot crops such as tomato accumulate substantial amounts of secondary xylem in their stems, particularly in the basal part. As plants progress from the vegetative phase to flowering and fruit development, secondary growth continues to provide mechanical support and facilitate transport. To uncover how secondary growth is regulated in the tomato stem, we used laser capture microdissection RNA-seq to establish tissue-specific transcriptomic profiles. This revealed that key regulators associated with wood formation in poplar are also acting in tomato. Furthermore, we found that the flowering regulators FUL2 and STM3 are substantially expressed in xylem tissue. Subsequent functional analysis identified FUL2 and STM3 as key repressors of secondary growth, with ful2 or stm3 knock-out mutants exhibiting strongly increased secondary growth in older tomato stems. Notably, a higher order mutant in which both ful2 and stm3 were knocked out displays a similar non-additive phenotype, indicating, together with yeast two-hybrid data showing physical interaction, that FUL2 and STM3 act together in a complex. The expression levels of both genes remain low until after the floral transition but strongly rise during subsequent stem development. Transcriptomic analyses in ful2, stm3, and wild-type stems at stages before and after detectable anatomical differences, showed that the FUL2-STM3 complex represses distinct sets of NAC and MYB candidate regulators associated with xylem development. Interestingly, FUL2 and STM3 control these regulators in a stage- and position-dependent way, with candidates showing upregulation only at later stages in mid-height stems being already upregulated at earlier stages in basal stem regions. Our findings provide a tissue-resolved transcriptomic resource for tomato stems and reveal a role for FUL2 and STM3 in limiting secondary xylem accumulation as stem development progresses.

items.title: Growing a Root from Its Genome : Emergent Tissue Layers and Zones in a GPU-Native Simulation of the Arabidopsis Root Tip
items.abstract: Models of the Arabidopsis root tip usually take its cell identities as given. Here we grow a root tip from a single genome. In a two-dimensional median section, every cell reads the same network of 62 genes (26 core genes from an earlier, unpublished model of callus and 36 added for the root) and starts with the same expression; the only spatial cues are the polarity of auxin transport, auxin from the shoot and the free surface. Identities and zones are never given to the simulation; they are read from gene expression. Cells are polygons of a shared mesh, relaxed towards mechanical equilibrium under turgor at every step. In 48 simulated hours, a tip-shaped template grows into a root of 3 000-4 500 cells with epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and stele in order along most of its length, SHORT-ROOT and SCARECROW in the endodermis, an auxin maximum, a quiescent centre and a cap at its tip, and meristem, elongation and mature zones. A WOX5 gate built from published interactions and one hypothesis keeps a quiescent centre to 48 h in 17 of 20 simulated roots that were not used for tuning (85%; Wilson 95% interval 64-95%; criteria fixed before the run), against 9 of 20 roots used for tuning, before the gate. The niche is not maintained beyond 48 h: grown on to 73 h, only 6 of these 20 roots still have a quiescent centre (30%; 15-52%). All pre-registered criteria hold in only 1 of 20 roots, because the quiescent centre is too wide at 0 h; without that count, 12 of 20. The meristem is too long, and cortical cells made after the start of growth elongate only three- to four-fold instead of eightto thirty-fold, a limit set in large part by the numerical growth scheme. Mutants are a major weakness: several look like their published phenotype, but an exploratory re-run of a mutant benchmark fixed in advance for our first model passes one of nine predictions. Nor does the root regenerate: cut near its tip, it re-forms an auxin maximum and a columella but no quiescent centre. On a first, simpler model and without any polarity cue, a mass of identical cells still sorts into concentric layers and, when PIN carriers follow the auxin flux, concentrates auxin into a few foci, but forms no stem-cell niche: the genome lacks a lateral inhibition between foci. We state the limitations and the next stages.

items.title: Evolutionary dynamics of the pan-centromere architecture in oaks
items.abstract: Centromeres ensure faithful chromosome segregation and genome stability, yet their DNA evolves rapidly, presenting a long-standing centromere paradox. Here we characterise the genomic and epigenomic architecture of >1,300 candidate centromeres from 111 high-quality Quercus (oak) genomes. We show that lineage-specific expansion of QuCEN146 satellite drives centromere turnover in oaks by displacing ancestral LTR-rich sequences into flanking regions, with genetic drift facilitating fixation of satellite-rich centromeres. Population-scale analyses in Q. serrata reveal extensive variation in satellite rich centromeres, generated by array expansion and contraction, strand-orientation shifts, and interspecific introgression. By contrast, LTR rich centromeres of Q. variabilis exhibit extremely low polymorphism and high collinearity across populations, sustained by suppressed local recombination, linked selection, and constrained LTR dynamics. We further demonstrate chromosome-independent evolutionary patterns for both satellite-rich and LTR-rich centromeres. Collectively, these findings demonstrate how evolutionary processes drive centromere turnover and shape contrasting centromeric sequence landscapes in forest trees.

items.title: SNAzzy: an image processing pipeline for investigating global Synchronous Network Activity
items.abstract: Genetically encoded fluorescent indicators are powerful tools for monitoring biological processes in live samples (Lin and Schnitzer 2016; Nakai, Ohkura, and Imoto 2001). When combined with a large field of view, a single time-lapse recording has the potential to capture many specimens, facilitating high-throughput data collection. However, this approach generates large, multidimensional datasets that are challenging to process and analyze. We present SNAzzy, a Python package for studying synchronous network activity (SNA) in Drosophila embryos via high-throughput microscopy. SNA is a hallmark of developing nervous systems (Wu, Kourdougli, and Portera-Cailliau 2024; Blankenship and Feller 2009; Akin and Zipursky 2020), often studied using genetically encoded calcium indicators to monitor neural activity in vivo. SNAzzy processes and analyzes time-lapse datasets taken from live samples using fluorescent widefield microscopy. Each dataset contains dozens of individual specimens in the same field of view and thousands of time points. The software offers individual specimen cropping for optimization of storage and processing, adaptive regions of interest for quantification of fluorescence and changes in morphology over time, a custom peak detection algorithm, and a graphical user interface for data visualization, curation, and dataset comparison. The code is available at https://github.com/ACRLab/snazzy.

items.title: Spiral ascent does not homogenize xylem transport: evidence from stable isotope tracing in Scots pine
items.abstract: Abstract The functional role of spiral grain remains debated. It is unclear whether spiral grain promotes tangential mixing of xylem resources or whether transport remains sectorial, as predicted by the pipe model of tree architecture. To address this question, we traced the natural uptake and transport of isotopically labelled water (2H) and dissolved nitrogen (as nitrate: K15NO3) in mature Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) growing in a boreal forest. A combined label solution was applied to a 1 m2 soil patch, and at the end of the season, five trees exhibiting clear label uptake were felled, and stem discs were collected along the stem axis. The most recent growth ring was analysed for incorporation of the 2H label, while 15N incorporation was assessed in current-year needles. We show that water taken up from the soil remains largely confined to discrete flow paths following the root trajectory, with minimal tangential spreading during transport through the stem. The labelled signal follows spiral grain but does not substantially mix across it, indicating that spiral grain does not function as an effective mechanism for lateral redistribution within the stem. Significant widening of the labelled sector occurs only upon reaching the crown, suggesting that increased connectivity at the branching level, rather than stem-level mixing, drives redistribution. In contrast, concurrently absorbed nitrogen is rapidly and mostly uniformly distributed across the canopy. This decoupling between water and nutrient pathways demonstrates that xylem transport is primarily source-driven and structurally constrained, whereas nutrient allocation operates at the whole-canopy level. By providing field-based evidence of tracer transport following natural root uptake, this study challenges the assumption that spiral grain enhances tangential mixing within the stem and highlights the need to account for sectorial transport pathways in ecohydrological studies.
items.authors: Magh RK, Lutter R, Henriksson N, Lim H, Lundmark T, Marshall JD

items.title: Phosphorylation Alters the Condensation State of the Potato Transcription Factor bZIP18 to Enhance Plant Immunity
items.abstract: Abstract Biomolecular condensates formed by transcription factors (TFs) via liquid-liquid phase separation enable precise spatiotemporal control of eukaryotic gene expression. Although phosphorylation is a well-established regulator of TF activity, its capacity to remodel condensate organization and transcriptional function in plant immunity remains largely undefined. Here, we report that pathogen-induced phosphorylation converts a pre-existing TF condensate into a dynamic transcriptional hub to enhance the immune response in potato. Upon infection by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans, the mitogen-activated protein kinase StMPK9 phosphorylates the TF StbZIP18 at the conserved residue threonine 337. This modification triggers rapid changes in the nuclear StbZIP18 condensates, transforming pre-existing condensates into numerous smaller assemblies. The phospho-null StbZIP18T337A mutant maintains its presence in low-activity condensates and compromises immunity, whereas the phospho-mimetic variant StbZIP18T337E constitutively forms active condensates and enhances resistance. The gene encoding the TF StMYB44 was identified as the direct downstream gene target of StbZIP18. TurboID-based proximity labeling revealed that both wild-type StbZIP18 and StbZIP18T337E, but not the phospho-null variant StbZIP18T337A, selectively interact with the transcriptional cofactor StMBF1c to form transcriptional activation hubs that drive defense gene expression, including StMYB44. Together, our findings establish that phosphorylation-directed condensate reprogramming operates as a tunable phase-separation switch, converting a low-activity assembly into a transcriptional amplifier. This study unveils a biophysical mechanism for signal amplification in plant immunity and provides insight into how post-translational modifications modulate transcriptional condensate function.
items.authors: Shi H, Chen Z, Chen Y, Sun Z, Li T, Joosten MHAJ, Du Y

items.title: Apoplastic sugars regulate stomatal opening and closure through integrated osmotic and metabolic mechanisms
items.abstract: Abstract The role of sucrose in stomatal regulation has been debated for more than a century, yet its underlying mechanism remains incompletely understood. Recent evidence indicates that apoplastic sucrose acts as a mesophyll-derived signal promoting stomatal opening in Arabidopsis, yet whether this mechanism operates in other species and under fluctuating environmental conditions, how sugars contribute to stomatal closure, and to what extent these responses depend on sucrose uptake and metabolism within guard cells (GCs) remain unresolved. Here, we carried out stomatal, metabolomics, and modeling analyses in leaves, the leaf apoplast, and GCs from tobacco wild-type and antisense lines for the GC SUCROSE TRANSPORTER 1 (NtSUT1). Daily variation in stomatal conductance (gs) was associated with the accumulation of sugars and organic acids in the apoplast. Stomatal opening and closure were associated with low and high concentrations of apoplastic sucrose over the diel course, respectively. Sugar feeding accelerated stomatal opening and closure in dark and light-adapted leaves, respectively, both in a concentration-dependent manner. NtSUT1 displayed alterations in apoplast and GC metabolite profiles, which resulted in lower gs and impaired sucrose-induced stomatal closure, compared with tobacco wild-type. Our findings suggest that apoplastic sugars and organic acids are associated with diurnal gs dynamics and that sugars can accelerate both stomatal opening and closure through an osmotic mechanism in the apoplast, and are also dependent on sucrose import and degradation within GCs. These results extend current models of stomatal regulation by demonstrating that sugars regulate both stomatal opening and closure through integrated osmotic and metabolic mechanisms.
items.authors: Freire FBS, Morais EG, Auler PA, Fan M, Antunes WC, Blatt MR, Lawson T, Gago J, Daloso DM

items.title: CsLUX-CsPME6/CsPMEI8/CsPMEI17 modulates pectin methylesterification to coordinate cold tolerance and growth in tea plants
items.abstract: Abstract Cell wall pectin methylesterification is critical for plant defense and development, yet how it coordinately regulates cold tolerance and growth in perennial crops remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that cold stress significantly reduces the degree of methylesterification (DM) of pectin in tea plants, concurrent with extensive remodeling of cellular and subcellular structures, including enhanced xylem development, altered mesophyll architecture, and impaired chloroplast morphology. Genome-wide analysis identifies 100 pectin methylesterase (PME) and 42 PME inhibitor (PMEI) genes, among which CsPME6, CsPMEI8, and CsPMEI17 exhibit cold-responsive expression and localize to the nucleus and apoplast. Functional studies demonstrate that CsPME6 positively regulates cold tolerance in tea plants, while CsPMEI8 and CsPMEI17 act as negative regulators. Mechanistically, CsPME6 elevates PME activity to lower pectin DM, whereas CsPMEI8 directly inhibit CsPME6 activity to maintain high pectin DM. Also, CsPMEI17 also negatively enhanced total PME activity to enhance the cold tolerance in tea plants. Notably, our findings suggested that the circadian clock component CsLUX directly binds to the LBS motifs in the promoters of these three genes, activating CsPME6 and repressing CsPMEI8/CsPMEI17 expression, which contributes to pectin methylesterification homeostasis. Besides, CsLUX-CsPME6/CsPMEI8/CsPMEI17 module also promote glutamate/γ-aminobutyric acid metabolism, leaf thickness, plant height, and root elongation in tea plants. Our findings underscore the importance of pectin methylesterification dynamics mediated by CsLUX-CsPME/PMEI involving cold tolerance and growth development in tea plants.
items.authors: Wang Y, Wu D, Su J, Wu Q, Zhao W, Zhu Y, Ma L, Song C, Tong W, Xia E

items.title: Phytochrome-Interacting Factors Regulate Katanin-Mediated Microtubule Severing to Control Hypocotyl/Mesocotyl Elongation During Skotomorphogenesis
items.abstract: Abstract The ability of plant seeds to emerge from the soil is achieved either by mesocotyl elongation in monocots or by hypocotyl elongation in dicots. Phytochrome-interacting factors (PIFs) are required for skotomorphogenesis, and microtubule remodeling plays a key driving role in cell elongation. However, the underlying cellular mechanisms in which PIFs act in concert with microtubule remodeling to control cell elongation during skotomorphogenesis remain unknown. Here, we demonstrate that in S. italica, the microtubule-severing defective mutant Siktn1 exhibits shortened mesocotyls and disorganized microtubule arrays. Similarly, in Arabidopsis, the microtubule-severing defective mutants lue1 and ktn80.1234 show shortened hypocotyls and abnormal microtubule arrays, which are caused by impaired microtubule severing. Intriguingly, pifq mutants exhibit shortened hypocotyls with reduced KTN1 and KTN80 expression, prompting us to investigate the relationship between PIFs and microtubule severing. Importantly, we found that PIFs transcriptionally activate KTN1 expression either in Arabidopsis or in S. italica. Further live-cell imaging confirmed that pifq mutants show reduced severing frequency and dwell time of the katanin complex. Taken together, these findings uncover a mechanism that PIFs orchestrate microtubule dynamics by regulating katanin activity, thereby fine-tuning cell elongation of hypocotyls/mesocotyls during skotomorphogenesis.
items.authors: Wang J, Hua R, Wang G, Wang X, Yan Y, Ren J, Yang H, Wang C, Zhang X, Tian J, Kong Z

items.title: Are plant annexins new components of protein complexes at membrane contact sites?
items.abstract: Abstract Annexins, as cytosolic and membrane-associated proteins, are essential for cellular processes in a wide range of eukaryotic organisms, spanning from humans to plants. They can bind calcium ions, phospholipids and cytoskeletal components, and thus play a crucial role in membrane organization, dynamics and trafficking, as well as in development and environmental stress responses of eukaryotes. A relatively new concept suggests that animal annexins AnxA6 and AnxA1 participate in protein complexes with other proteins, such as Drp1, Rab GTPase 7, TBC1D15, or FIS1, that are important for the establishment and function of membrane contact sites (MCSs) between several subcellular compartments. Plant annexins show diverse subcellular localizations, including putative MCSs between organelles, but their participation in MCS protein complexes is unknown. Despite limited homology with the MCS-localized animal annexins AnxA6 and AnxA1, bioinformatic analyses, AlphaFold-Multimer modelling and fluorescence confocal microscopy support a possible role for Arabidopsis annexins in MCS formation and function. All eight Arabidopsis annexins are predicted to have FFAT motifs that may be potentially important for MCSs formation between endoplasmic reticulum and other organelles. Moreover, there are plant dynamin, Rab GTPase, TBC1D15, and FIS1 and VAMP homologs, which might form functional complexes with some plant annexins in MCSs. This update provides a new perspective on plant annexins, presenting them as new putative players in protein complexes important for organellar interactions in MCSs.
items.authors: Šamajová O, Gentric E, Takáč T, Hegerová K, Medelská M, Šamaj J

items.title: Verticillium dahliae CAP-containing effectors hijack the β-subunit of the SnRK1 complex to suppress plant immunity
items.abstract: Abstract The soil-borne fungus Verticillium dahliae causes Verticillium wilt, a devastating disease threatening global cotton production. Like many pathogens, V. dahliae delivers effectors into plant cells to facilitate infection. The CAP (Cysteine-rich secretory protein, Antigen 5 and Pathogenesis-related protein 1) superfamily represents a typical group of secretory proteins that function as virulence factors and modulate plant immunity. Although V. dahliae utilizes CAP proteins to disrupt plant immune responses, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we initially screened the targets of VdCAP1 in cotton and demonstrated that it interacts with the β-subunit of SnRK1 complex both in vivo and in vitro. Silencing GhSnRK1β1 significantly enhanced susceptibility to V. dahliae infection, indicating its positive role in cotton defense against the pathogen. Further investigation revealed that VdCAP1 disrupts the interaction between SnRK1β1 and the core α-subunit of the SnRK1 complex and reduces the nuclear accumulation of GhSnRK1β1. Notably, GhSnRK1β1 exhibits opposing roles depending on its subcellular localization. Nuclear-localized GhSnRK1β1 promotes flg22-triggered ROS accumulation, whereas cytoplasmic-localized GhSnRK1β1 suppresses ROS accumulation. Furthermore, co-expression of VdCAP1 also promotes GhSnRK1β1-mediated ROS scavenging. Another secretory protein, VdCAP3, which functions as a plant immunity suppressor, interacts with GhSnRK1β1 and similarly restricts its nuclear accumulation to suppress plant immunity. Collectively, these findings indicated that VdCAP1/3 suppresses plant immunity by targeting SnRK1β1, thereby increasing V. dahliae pathogenicity.
items.authors: Wang J, Sheng R, Zhang Q, Bao X, Yang X, Dai X, Subbarao KV, Chen J, Zhang D

items.title: Plant potassium channel β -subunits confer antiviral defense via disrupting potyviral 6K2-mediated vesicle maturation and trafficking
items.abstract: Abstract Potyviruses constitute the largest known group of plant RNA viruses. Their 6K2 protein is an integral membrane protein that induces the formation of vesicular structures, which support viral RNA replication and act as vehicles for intracellular movement. While multiple host proteins are known to regulate either viral replication or movement, it remains largely unclear whether and how a single host protein can coordinately modulate both processes. Here, we identify NbKNB1, a Nicotiana benthamiana homolog of the plant potassium channel β-subunit. Genetic assays demonstrate that NbKNB1 confers antiviral activity against turnip mosaic virus (TuMV). NbKNB1 localizes predominantly to the plasma membrane in healthy cells, but relocalizes to 6K2-induced viral replication complexes during TuMV infection. Biochemical analyses show that NbKNB1 directly interacts with 6K2, disrupting 6K2 self-association and impairing the maturation of 6K2-tagged vesicles. NbKNB1 also competes with the viral cylindrical inclusion (CI) protein for 6K2 binding, thereby inhibiting TuMV cell-to-cell movement. A 6K2-binding-deficient mutant, NbKNB1Δ270-279, fails to restrict both viral replication and intercellular movement, confirming that direct interaction with 6K2 is required for NbKNB1-mediated suppression of TuMV infection. Moreover, NbKNB1 and its maize homolog ZmKZB1 also reduce infection by other potyviruses. Collectively, these findings reveal a novel antiviral strategy in which plant potassium channel β-subunit homologs target the viral 6K2 protein to counteract potyvirus infection, and provide a promising target for antiviral breeding.
items.authors: Yan Q, Gu R, Xiao M, Wang H, Wang L, Lin W, Chen C, Xie J, Song Z, Bao Y, Du K, Zhang Z, Yang X, Xie J, Zhou T

items.title: Soil engineering by an invasive ant reprograms plant growth–defense trade‐offs to entrench a tripartite mutualism
items.abstract: Summary Ants are ubiquitous ecosystem engineers, yet the mechanisms through which their nesting activity regulates mutualistic interactions remain elusive. Here, we provide evidence consistent with the hypothesis that ant nesting initiates a soil–plant–herbivore cascade that reinforces a tripartite mutualism. Using the invasive fire ant Solenopsis invicta as a model system in both laboratory and field settings, we show that ant nesting increases soil nitrate and ammonium concentrations, which are associated with enhanced plant growth. These nesting‐related changes coincide with shifts in the host plant's hormonal signaling network: auxin signaling is systemically elevated, whereas salicylic acid defense pathways and jasmonate signal transduction are suppressed. Plants associated with ant nests exhibit compromised defense responses to aphid herbivory. This shift toward a growth‐biased physiology supports larger aphid populations, which in turn provide increased carbohydrate rewards for ants, augmenting ant colony survival and brood biomass. Collectively, our findings suggest a potential terrestrial feedback loop in which ants indirectly enhance their own performance through nesting‐associated changes in soil nutrients and plant physiology, which ultimately benefit a mutualist herbivore. In doing so, this study establishes a tripartite ant–plant–herbivore mutualism that extends beyond the ‘food‐for‐protection’ paradigm as classically defined.
items.authors: Hu C, Ma R, Nelson AS, Wan J, Hu Y, Li L, Xu L, Tan W, Niu C, Zhou A

items.title: OsERF27 ‐ OsPLT4 regulatory module and ROS equilibrium control temporospatial rice crown root patterning
items.abstract: Summary In rice ( Oryza sativa ), the root architecture is heavily shaped by shoot‐borne crown roots that arise from the phytomers at the stem base. Each phytomer typically generates two spatially distinct crown root populations – lower/proximal and upper/distal crown roots – that also emerge temporally, with the proximal roots forming first. The mechanisms that coordinate this temporospatial patterning, however, remain poorly understood. Here, we identify an AP2/ERF gene OsERF27 which is differentially expressed between proximal and distal crown root primordia and is specifically required for the timely development of proximal roots. We further show that OsPLT4 functions downstream of OsERF27 , defining an OsERF27‐OsPLT4 regulatory module that drives the outgrowth and emergence of proximal crown roots. Interestingly, we uncover a requirement for reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis in crown root development: Loss‐of‐function mutants display disturbed ROS accumulation pattern and sensitized root formation to ROS perturbation, indicating that this module promotes root emergence by spatially maintaining optimal redox balance. Together, our findings reveal a multi‐layered regulatory network that integrates genetic elements with positional cues with redox control to pattern distinct crown root populations. Our study highlights how localized developmental programmes scale to shape root system architecture for tuning plant form and function in grasses.

items.title: The CitRWP–CsWUS regulatory axis governs citrus plant regeneration in association with chromatin remodeling
items.abstract: Summary Plant regeneration underpins crop genetic improvement, yet its regulatory mechanism remains poorly characterized in woody fruit trees. The RWP‐RK domain‐containing (RKD) transcription factor CitRWP acts as a pleiotropic regulator of nucellar polyembryony and somatic embryogenesis (SE) in citrus, but its downstream molecular network remains elusive. We demonstrate that CsWUS, a core stem cell regulator, is a direct downstream target of CitRWP. CitRWP binds to the CsWUS promoter to activate its transcription. Additionally, CitRWP interacts with the SWItch/Sucrose Non‐Fermentable (SWI/SNF) chromatin‐remodeling ATPase SPLAYED (SYD), synergistically enhancing CsWUS activation, while chromatin accessibility at the CsWUS locus is enhanced upon CitRWP overexpression. We further uncover that CsWUS negatively regulates CitRWP expression via a feedback loop. CsWUS overexpression promotes SE in recalcitrant citrus callus, but causes abnormal meristem proliferation and impairs shoot organogenesis from epicotyl segments. CsWUS greatly enhanced in planta transformation efficiency in the model citrus. This study establishes the CitRWP – CsWUS regulatory axis as a central module that coordinates multiple developmental fate transitions in association with chromatin remodeling, providing novel insights into the mechanisms of cellular totipotency and plant regeneration.

items.title: Arabidopsis thaliana BOLA proteins, new actors in plant growth and iron homeostasis
items.abstract: SUMMARY The universal iron–sulfur (Fe‐S) clusters embedded in proteins support numerous fundamental biological processes. However, many proteins involved in Fe‐S assembly machineries remain poorly characterized in plants. Here, we revealed that BOLA1 and BOLA4, two members of the BOLA family previously described as Fe‐S assembly factors in various organisms, are critical growth regulators that play a role in Fe homeostasis in Arabidopsis thaliana . Expression analyses showed that BOLA1 and BOLA4 are ubiquitously expressed across most Arabidopsis tissues. Using protoplast transfection assays, we also demonstrated that both BOLA‐GFP fusion proteins localize to chloroplasts and mitochondria. Mutant analyses revealed that while single bola1 or bola4 knock‐out mutants are phenotypically indistinguishable from the wild type, double bola1 bola4 mutants display severe growth defects, including early growth arrest of the primary root. Notably, this phenotype was rescued by grafting a wild‐type root system onto the bola1 bola4 aerial part. Fe quantification, Perls staining, and RT‐qPCR analyses further demonstrated that bola1 bola4 double mutants exhibit altered Fe distribution and Fe‐homeostasis‐related gene expression. Overall, our findings show that BOLA1 and BOLA4 act redundantly to maintain primary root growth and rosette development and are essential players in Fe signaling and partitioning in Arabidopsis.

items.title: An S‐domain receptor‐like kinase regulates auxin distribution and root gravitropism via MPK signaling in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: SUMMARY Root system architecture (RSA) varies across environments and plays essential roles in plant adaptive growth. Auxin and its polar transport have been found to be key players in the regulation of RSA. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of RSA in fluctuating environments remain unclear. Using a forward genetic screen for root mutants under gravitropism interference conditions in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana , we revealed that HYPERSENSITIVE TO IBUPROFEN1 ( HIB1 ) regulates root gravitropic growth and RSA by modulating auxin distribution in Arabidopsis. The hib1 seedlings presented defects in primary root elongation, lateral root organogenesis, and the root gravitropic response because of abnormal auxin distribution. Notably, the gravitropic defects of hib1 roots were correlated with increased MPK6 activity and could be rescued by loss‐of‐function mpk6 mutation. Furthermore, cell biological results revealed that HIB1 regulated PIN protein polar distribution and abundance at the plasma membrane, indicating that HIB1 is involved in polar auxin transport and the subsequent auxin response. Indeed, genetic perturbation of HIB1 results in impaired gravitropic root growth. Our work revealed that the HIB1‐auxin module regulates root gravitropism and RSA, providing insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying adaptive root growth.

items.title: Altered plastidial fatty‐acid condensation is associated with changes in membrane composition and postembryonic leaf development in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: SUMMARY Membrane lipid composition is fundamental to organelle structure and environmental adaptation, yet how plastidial fatty acid metabolism influences developmental plasticity remains poorly understood. We examined the effects of sustained elevation of the plastidial fatty‐acid enzymes KASII (β‐ketoacyl‐ACP synthase II) and SSI2 (Δ9 stearoyl‐ACP desaturase 2) in Arabidopsis thaliana using lipidomic, ultrastructural, cellular, molecular, and physiological analyses. KASII overexpressing plants (KASIIox), but not SSI2 overexpressing plants (SSI2ox), increased carbon 18‐containing lipid species and exhibited reduced plastidial galactolipids together with increased extraplastidial phospholipids. KASIIox plants displayed enlarged chloroplasts with disrupted thylakoid organization, impaired palisade differentiation, altered mesophyll patterning, and reduced seed coat mucilage. Under low light, KASIIox plants failed to exhibit the characteristic petiole elongation observed in control and SSI2ox plants, accompanied by altered phyB and PIF4 protein abundance. Exogenous gibberellin intensified, whereas inhibition of gibberellin biosynthesis partially alleviated KASIIox leaf and cellular phenotypes. Together, these findings associate sustained KASII elevation with changes in membrane lipid composition, chloroplast architecture, light‐responsive growth, and postembryonic leaf development, supporting a link between plastidial fatty‐acid metabolism and developmental responses to light and gibberellin availability.

items.title: Plant Receptor‐Like Kinase‐Mediated Drought Stress Response Mechanism—From Root Sensing to Stomatal Regulation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Drought is a multifaceted environmental constraint that alters water dynamics across the soil‐plant‐atmosphere system. In order to survive under drought stress, plants must respond at several levels from cellular signalling to whole‐plant hydraulic regulation. Although receptor‐like kinases (RLKs) have been reported to play important roles in these responses, they are often studied within individual molecular pathways rather than as integrators of environmental and physiological processes. Here, we review RLK‐mediated drought signalling organised across three interconnected spatial scales. At the root–soil interface, RLKs perceive osmotic and mechanical cues to regulate root architecture, aquaporin dynamics and apoplastic barrier formation, thereby tuning root hydraulic conductivity. Over long distances, RLK‐peptide modules and reactive oxygen species waves transmit water‐deficit signals from roots to shoots via xylem transport and cell‐to‐cell propagation, while RLK‐dependent vascular differentiation preserves hydraulic safety. In leaves, RLKs modulate stomatal aperture through ion‐channel regulation, ROS‐calcium signalling, cell‐wall mechanosensing and developmental reprogramming of stomatal density. Importantly, we highlight how these pathways operate across distinct temporal scales—from rapid electrochemical responses to long‐term anatomical remodelling—and identify key unresolved questions, including how signalling specificity is achieved among redundant RLK members and how hydraulic and biochemical cues are integrated. By linking RLK‐mediated signalling to whole‐plant physiological responses, this review offers potential avenues for enhancing crop drought resilience through targeted modulation of RLK pathways.

items.title: Reciprocal Regulatory Interactions Between Class I TCP Transcription Factors and ABA Signalling Balance Growth and Stress Responses in Arabidopsis
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Abscisic acid (ABA) plays a critical role in regulating plant responses to abiotic stress by modulating various physiological processes through complex molecular networks. TEOSINTE BRANCHED1/CYCLOIDEA/PROLIFERATING CELL FACTORS (TCP) transcription factors are known developmental regulators, but their roles in ABA signalling and abiotic stress responses remain poorly understood. We addressed this question by analysing the closely related Arabidopsis thaliana class I TCPs TCP14 and TCP15 using a variety of genetic and molecular approaches. We found that TCP14 and TCP15 negatively influence ABA and salt stress responses. They function by directly activating genes encoding negative regulators of ABA signalling, such as ABA‐INSENSITIVE FIVE‐BINDING PROTEIN 2 ( AFP2 ), thereby suppressing the expression of ABA‐INSENSITIVE 5 ( ABI5 ) and downstream ABA‐responsive genes to inhibit ABA responses under non‐stressful conditions. Notably, the TCPs are targets of ABA‐mediated regulation, as ABA negatively affects TCP14 and TCP15 protein abundance, providing a mechanism to limit TCP‐dependent transcriptional growth responses and de‐repress ABA‐signalling pathways during times of stress. We propose that the antagonistic interplay between class I TCPs and ABA may serve to fine‐tune plant growth and stress responses according to environmental conditions, positioning TCP14 and TCP15 as crucial players in balancing plant developmental progression and stress adaptation.

items.title: Single‐Nucleus Transcriptomics Reveals Cell Type Specific Defence Responses and Identifies AhWRKY40 as a Key Regulator of Peanut Resistance to Sclerotium rolfsii
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Peanut stem rot caused by Sclerotium rolfsii is a devastating soil borne disease that severely constrains peanut production worldwide. Despite its economic importance, highly resistant peanut cultivars are still largely unavailable, and the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying peanut resistance remain poorly understood. We obtained a total of 29,308 high‐quality nuclei, annotated five major cell types, and detected 52,819 expressed genes. Comparative analysis revealed widespread transcriptional reprogramming and a predominance of downregulated genes in response to pathogen infection, accompanied by a substantial reduction in cell abundance across all cell populations. Notably, epidermal cells harboured the highest proportion of disease resistance genes. Pseudotime trajectory analysis further demonstrated that S. rolfsii infection altered cellular transcriptional states and induced cell type specific immune reprogramming. Integrative analyses combining gene coexpression, pseudotime dynamics, virtual knockout, and transgenic validation consistently identified AhWRKY40 as a key regulatory factor associated with disease resistance. Overexpression of AhWRKY40 enhanced resistance to S. rolfsii and was accompanied by increased accumulation of jasmonic acid (JA) and salicylic acid (SA), suggesting its involvement in hormone‐mediated defence responses. Collectively, our study provides new insights into the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying peanut resistance to stem rot, identifies AhWRKY40 as a promising candidate gene for disease resistance, and establishes a valuable resource for functional genomics and molecular breeding to improve southern blight resistance in peanut.

items.title: Everything, Everywhere, not at Once: How Abscisic Acid Shapes Root Responses to Salt Stress
items.abstract: Abstract Abscisic acid (ABA) is a central hormone in plants to regulate salinity response, which is an increasing threat to plant growth and crop productivity. This review focuses on the role of ABA in salinity response in roots – an essential organ for plant nutrition acquisition and anchorage. It provides an overview of how ABA responses in roots vary across time, tissues, and salt intensity, and why these dynamics are essential for understanding root salt response. We present ABA-related gene transcriptomic profiles based on public transcriptomic datasets generated from salt-treated seedlings, including genes involved in biosynthesis, catabolism, (de)conjugation, transport and signalling of ABA. We discuss how genes and interaction networks governing each of these steps are coordinated in spatial-temporal, and salt-dose dependent manners. Finally, we highlight how ABA can potentially act as secondary signalling wave to regulate root salt responses, including the salt-avoidance response—halotropism.

items.title: FaWRKY7 modulates jasmonate signaling responses and enhances strawberry fruit resistance to Botrytis cinerea
items.abstract: Abstract WRKY transcription factors and jasmonic acid (JA) signaling are essential for plant responses to stress, but their roles in strawberry resistance to Botrytis cinerea remain unclear. Here, we investigated the function of FaWRKY7 in strawberry fruit and transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana. FaWRKY7 expression was significantly induced at 72 h after B. cinerea inoculation. Transient overexpression of FaWRKY7 enhanced strawberry fruit resistance to B. cinerea, whereas silencing increased susceptibility. Similarly, FaWRKY7-overexpressing Arabidopsis plants showed enhanced resistance to B. cinerea and greater responsiveness to exogenous methyl jasmonate (MeJA), although basal levels of free JA, JA-Ile, and OPDA were not detectably altered in non-inoculated samples. Pharmacological assays further showed that FaWRKY7-mediated resistance was maintained under MeJA treatment and only partially reduced by Jarin-1, an inhibitor of JA-Ile formation, indicating that this effect is only partially dependent on JA-Ile formation. Mechanistically, DAP-seq, yeast one-hybrid, EMSA, and dual-luciferase assays showed that FaWRKY7 directly binds to the promoters of FaJAZ4 and FaJAZ8 and represses their transcription. These findings indicate that FaWRKY7 enhances resistance to B. cinerea, at least in part by directly repressing FaJAZ4 and FaJAZ8 and thereby modulating jasmonate signaling responses.

items.title: β-GlcY treatment alters transcriptome dynamics and auxin distribution during microspore embryogenesis in Brassica napus
items.abstract: Abstract Microspore embryogenesis (ME) is a classical model for plant cell fate reprogramming, involving extensive transcriptional and structural reorganization. Arabinogalactan proteins (AGPs), key components of the cell wall interface, have been implicated in ME, but their effects during early cell fate reprogramming remain unclear. Here, in Brassica napus, using morphological observation, embryogenic reporters, and stage-specific transcriptomics, we show that β-D-glucosyl Yariv (β-GlcY) treatment, perturbing AGP-related functions, is associated with impaired activation and spatial distribution of embryogenic markers. Transcriptome profiling reveals that the first 24 h after culture represent a major stage of AGP-associated transcriptional responses. β-GlcY treatment attenuates developmental and chromatin-associated pathways while upregulating stress-responsive and metabolic programs. Notably, 24 h marks a key transition, with altered expression of genes involved in rRNA processing, chromatin organization, and sister chromatid cohesion, suggesting AGPs help establish a permissive transcriptional and chromatin state for fate conversion. Consistently, β- GlcY treatment is associated with altered cell wall organization, auxin distribution, and PIN1 polarization, suggesting a potential connection between extracellular matrix perturbation and polarity establishment. Together, these results suggest that β-GlcY treatment is associated with changes in extracellular structure, transcriptional reprogramming, and hormone-mediated polarity during the acquisition of embryogenic competence of early ME.

items.title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root
items.abstract: Abstract Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.
